Call to non-existent no-arg isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() breaks compilation

`UsernameForm.authenticate` calls `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` with no arguments. The only method added in the superclass `UsernamePasswordForm` is `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)`, and no no-arg overload exists anywhere in the hierarchy. The services module will not compile, so neither the fix nor the new tests can run. The call should pass the current user, e.g. `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())`.

true_positives.golden_comment: With isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user) requiring user != null, authenticate(...) will not call webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context) on the initial login page where context.getUser() is still null, so conditional passkey UI will not be set up for first-time passkey login. Consider whether this should also be enabled when no user has been selected yet so ID-less passkey authentication on the initial login form continues to work.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isConditionalPasskeysEnabled requires user != null, disabling passkeys on normal login and enabling them for every re-auth

The new helper returns `webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled() && user != null`. Before this PR, the conditional UI was filled only when no user was selected yet (the normal identity-first login). It is used in `authenticate()` (line 115) and in `challenge(context, error, field)` (line 137), and with this condition:
(1) On a fresh login where `context.getUser()` is null, `fillContextForm` is never called. The webauthn challenge and conditional UI are no longer rendered, so passkey login is broken for all first-time and logged-out logins.
(2) During re-authentication it returns true for any identified user, so the passkey UI is shown even to users with no passkey credential.
The intended condition is `user == null || user.credentialManager().isConfiguredFor(webauthnAuth.getCredentialType())`.

false_positives.candidate:
Re-auth test for user without passkey disables passkeys realm-wide, so the per-user check is never tested

`reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey` sets `setWebAuthnPolicyPasskeysEnabled(Boolean.FALSE)` for the whole realm. The webauthn form is therefore absent simply because the feature is off, not because the user lacks a passkey. Yet the inline comment at line 304 says passkeys are unavailable "as this user does not have passkey".

The important case is never exercised: passkeys enabled in the realm, and a user without a passkey credential re-authenticating with prompt=login. That case is exactly where the `user != null` logic in `UsernamePasswordForm.isConditionalPasskeysEnabled` misbehaves. The test should keep passkeys enabled and assert the webauthn form is absent for test-user@localhost.

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative-offset branch slices a QuerySet with a negative index, causing an unhandled error

With `enable_advanced_features=True` and a client-supplied cursor such as `0:-10:0`, the code runs `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative `start_offset`.

Django QuerySets do not support negative indexing; they raise `ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported.")`. The comment claiming "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is false.

`Endpoint.paginate` only converts `BadPaginationError` into a 400. So any client can trigger a 500 by crafting the cursor.

The stated intent, "access to data beyond normal pagination bounds", is also not a legitimate feature. Negative offsets should be rejected with `BadPaginationError`, as `OffsetPaginator` and `ChainPaginator` already do.

true_positives.golden_comment: When requests are authenticated with API keys or org auth tokens (which have user_id=None), organization_context.member is None. Line 71 attempts to access organization_context.member.has_global_access without checking if member is None, causing an AttributeError crash when optimized_pagination=true is used, even though the request passed all permission checks with valid org:write scope.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unconditional `organization_context.member.has_global_access` crashes when there is no member

`enable_advanced` is computed on every request, even when `optimized_pagination` is not requested. `RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` is optional. It is `None` for callers that pass `OrganizationAuditPermission` without an org membership, for example:
- staff users who are not superusers
- legacy API keys / token-authenticated requests where `request.user` is anonymous

For those callers, `None.has_global_access` raises `AttributeError`, so the previously working default `DateTimePaginator` path now returns a 500.

Fix: guard on `member is not None`, and only evaluate this when `use_optimized` is true.

true_positives.golden_comment: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator cannot handle the datetime sort key, so the optimized path always fails

The audit log endpoint uses `OptimizedCursorPaginator` with `order_by="-datetime"`. Its `get_item_key` calls `math.floor`/`math.ceil` directly on `item.datetime`. That raises `TypeError: must be real number, not datetime`.

As soon as the first page has any rows, `build_cursor` → `_build_next_values` calls `key(results[0])` and the request fails with a 500.

`value_from_cursor` also returns the raw integer cursor value. `build_queryset` then emits `sentry_auditlogentry.datetime <= <int>`, which Postgres rejects, so any request carrying a cursor also errors.

The result is that the whole `optimized_pagination=true` path is unusable. This contradicts the docstring's claim of backward compatibility: cursors issued by `DateTimePaginator` (millisecond timestamps) cannot be consumed here.

Fix: reuse `DateTimePaginator`'s key and cursor conversion, e.g. subclass `DateTimePaginator` instead of re-implementing it.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Importing non-existent OptimizedCursorPaginator

false_positives.candidate:
Admin gating uses the raw superuser flag and `has_global_access`, which is not an admin check

The feature is described as being for "authorized administrators", but the gate does not enforce that.

`request.user.is_superuser` bypasses Sentry's active-superuser-session requirement; the codebase uses `is_active_superuser(request)` for this.

`has_global_access` is also true for every member of an org with open membership (`allow_joinleave`), not just owners or managers.

As a result, the extra paginator behaviour, including the negative-offset path, is exposed more broadly than intended.

BasePaginator change still passes negative offsets to the QuerySet for prev cursors

`start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` silently clamps negative offsets for next cursors. This behaviour change affects every endpoint using `BasePaginator`.

For prev cursors it still passes the negative value to `queryset[start_offset:stop]`, which raises `ValueError` from Django and returns a 500 for a crafted cursor such as `123:-5:1`.

The accompanying comment ("This is safe because the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions") is incorrect.

Fix: raise `BadPaginationError` for any negative offset.

Comment claims negative offsets are supported, but nothing changed

The added comment says Cursor now allows negative offsets for "efficient reverse pagination". No code was changed: `int(offset)` already accepted negatives.

No paginator actually supports negative offsets either; Django slicing rejects them, and other paginators raise `BadPaginationError`.

The comment misleads future maintainers into thinking negative offsets are a supported, safe contract.

New paginator and endpoint branch have no tests

No tests were added for:
- `OptimizedCursorPaginator`
- the `optimized_pagination=true` branch of the audit log endpoint
- the modified `BasePaginator` offset handling

A single request through the new branch with at least one audit log entry would have surfaced the `TypeError` on the datetime key. A cursor with a negative offset would have surfaced the Django `ValueError`.

The new class also duplicates `BasePaginator.get_result` almost verbatim, which increases the surface that needs coverage.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset branch in get_result() passes cursor.offset directly as start_offset to queryset slicing when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
User-controlled negative offsets are passed to QuerySet slicing; the "safe" claim is false

With `enable_advanced_features` set and `cursor.offset < 0`, which the client controls through a cursor string like `0:-50:0`, the code runs `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative start. Django QuerySets do not support negative indexing and raise `ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported.")`, so any such request is a 500. The comment says the ORM "properly handles negative slicing automatically"; that is wrong. The comment also says this "enables access to data beyond normal pagination bounds" and is "safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level". That describes a deliberate bound-bypass feature driven by untrusted input, which should not exist. Negative offsets should be rejected with `BadPaginationError` (400), as `OffsetPaginator` does.

true_positives.golden_comment: In BasePaginator.get_result(), when cursor.is_prev is True, it sets start_offset = offset without clamping, allowing negative offset values to be passed to queryset slicing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
BasePaginator still slices with negative offsets for prev cursors; comment is misleading

`start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` only clamps non-prev cursors. A prev cursor with a negative offset, such as `123:-5:1`, still reaches `queryset[negative:...]` and raises `ValueError`, giving a 500 instead of a 400. Next cursors with a negative offset are now silently coerced to the first page instead of being rejected. The comment says negative offsets enable bidirectional pagination and that the queryset handles boundaries, but neither is true. The same misleading comment was added to `Cursor.__init__` in `utils/cursors.py` with no code change. Validate and reject negative offsets instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key uses floor/ceil on a datetime key (order_by='-datetime'), causing TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator cannot handle the datetime key it is used with

The audit-log endpoint uses `OptimizedCursorPaginator` with `order_by="-datetime"`. However, `get_item_key` calls `math.floor`/`math.ceil` directly on the field value, which is a `datetime`, and that raises `TypeError`. `build_cursor` calls the key on the first result whenever any results exist, so every non-empty optimized request returns a 500. `value_from_cursor` also returns the raw integer cursor value instead of converting it to a datetime as `DateTimePaginator` does. A follow-up cursor would therefore generate `datetime <= <int>` SQL, which fails in Postgres. The optimized path is non-functional for this endpoint.

true_positives.golden_comment: Accessing .has_global_access on organization_context.member can raise an AttributeError when organization_context is None, particularly for non-superuser non-member users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unconditional access to organization_context.member crashes when requester is not an org member

`enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` runs on every request, not only when `optimized_pagination=true` is passed. `organization_context.member` is None when the caller is not an org member, for example staff users or API-key/token auth where `request.user` is anonymous. If the caller is not a superuser, this raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'has_global_access'`. The default audit-log listing path, which worked before this PR, then returns a 500 for those callers. At minimum, evaluate this only when `use_optimized` is true and guard against `member is None`.

false_positives.candidate:
"Admin-only" gate uses raw is_superuser and has_global_access, neither of which identifies administrators

The comment says advanced pagination is limited to authorized administrators, but the check does not enforce that. `request.user.is_superuser` ignores whether the user has an active superuser session; Sentry normally requires `is_active_superuser(request)`. `member.has_global_access` is true for ordinary members whenever the org has open membership enabled, and for any role with global access. So regular members can opt into the paginator that is explicitly designed to read "beyond normal pagination bounds" via user-controlled negative offsets. Use a proper permission or role check, or drop the feature.

No test covers the new insert-time eviction

The core behavior change, trimming a segment to 1000 spans via ZPOPMIN by `end_timestamp_precise` including after merges via ZUNIONSTORE, has no test. The existing tests only add `end_timestamp_precise=1700000000.0` to fixtures, with every span sharing the same score, so the eviction order is never exercised. Add a test inserting more than 1000 spans with distinct timestamps across batches and merges, and assert which spans survive. Similarly, the new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` and the audit-log `optimized_pagination` path have no tests, which is how the datetime TypeError and negative-slicing crash went unnoticed.

Redirect-depth limit silently reduced from 10000 to 1000

The loop bound for following span redirects drops from 10000 to 1000, and the comment explaining the consequence was removed. The consequence is that segment trees deeper than the limit are not joined correctly. This behavior change is unrelated to eviction, is not mentioned in the PR, and now applies to much shallower trees.

Spans beyond 1000 are silently evicted with no metric or log

`zpopmin set_key span_count - 1000` permanently drops the earliest-ending spans of a segment with no visibility. The removed Python code at least emitted `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` and logged an error. Now there is no signal that data was discarded. Eviction is by `end_timestamp_precise` only, so it can also remove the segment/root span when children end after it, while the `hrs` flag still marks the segment as having a root. Return the evicted count from the script and emit a metric in `process_spans`.

Switching span-buf:s:* keys from SET to ZSET breaks on existing keys during deploy (WRONGTYPE)

Segment keys written by the previous version are plain Redis sets with TTL up to `redis_ttl` (3600s). After deploy, `ZADD` here, `ZCARD`/`ZUNIONSTORE` in add-buffer.lua, and `ZSCAN` in `_load_segment_data` will hit those keys and fail with `WRONGTYPE`. During a rolling deploy, old consumers likewise run `SADD`/`SCARD` against new ZSET keys. Pipelines raise on the first error, so both the process step and the flusher will crash-loop on any batch or flush touching such a key, potentially for up to an hour until the keys expire. This needs a migration or compat strategy, such as new key prefixes, type-checking with fallback, or draining or flushing the buffer before rollout.

ZUNIONSTORE uses default SUM aggregation, corrupting scores for duplicate payloads

`zunionstore set_key 2 set_key span_key` (and the same call at line 53) defaults to `AGGREGATE SUM`. If the same span payload exists in both sets, for example after Kafka redelivery or reprocessing a batch, its score becomes the sum of the timestamps (about 2x the end timestamp). That breaks the end-timestamp ordering the new `zpopmin` eviction relies on, and makes such spans effectively un-evictable. Use `AGGREGATE MAX` (or MIN) to keep a real timestamp.

max_segment_spans is now dead configuration; limit is hard-coded to 1000 in Lua

The `max_segment_spans` constructor parameter (default 1001) is no longer read anywhere, because the span-count check was removed from `_load_segment_data`. The actual limit is a hard-coded `1000` in add-buffer.lua, which also differs from the old default. Callers configuring `max_segment_spans` will get no effect. Pass the limit as an ARGV to the script, or remove the parameter.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling decision uses outer `dataset` and the raw request query instead of the dataset/query actually being executed

Inside `_get_event_stats` the eligibility check is passed the closed-over `dataset`, not the `scoped_dataset` argument. The helper also inspects `request.GET["query"]` rather than the `query` argument.

In the dashboard discover-split path, `_get_event_stats` is called with `discover` and a rewritten query (`({query}) AND !event.type:transaction`, or ERROR_EVENTS split widgets). The outer `dataset` there is always metrics_performance or metrics_enhanced_performance, so `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` returns False. Error-only results for split widgets are therefore never upsampled, while the same query from a non-dashboard request is.

The same mismatch can let a transactions-only sub-query be judged by the original request's query text.

Fix: pass `scoped_dataset` and the effective `query` into the eligibility check.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.

false_positives.candidate:
"Performance" cache adds a remote cache round-trip to every events-stats call

`options.get` is normally served from an in-process cache, so the check it guards is a cheap list-membership test. Wrapping it in `cache.get` and `cache.set` (memcached/redis) adds a network round-trip per `_get_event_stats` call, which is several calls per request in the dashboard-split and comparison paths.

The check also runs even when no `count()` column is requested. Net effect: added latency and cache load with no benefit.

60s eligibility cache is never invalidated and contradicts the 'fresh read' contract

The eligibility result is cached for 60 seconds per org and project set. `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is never called anywhere, and it cannot practically be: invalidation needs every project-id combination that was cached, but option changes are not tied to orgs or project sets.

After a project is removed from `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist`, for example to roll back a bad rollout, its counts stay inflated for up to a minute. That inconsistency is per project set.

The docstring of `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` says the allowlist is read fresh each time "to ensure we always have the latest configuration state", which the caching wrapper defeats. The cache key also relies on the Python `hash()` of the project tuple, so distinct project sets can in principle share an entry.

Options:
- Drop the cache, since options are already cached in-process.
- Wire up invalidation and use the full sorted id list or a stable digest in the key.

Error-focused detection is a raw substring match and also matches negated `!event.type:error`

`_is_error_focused_query` returns True whenever the lowercased query contains `event.type:error`. That is also true for `!event.type:error`, which explicitly excludes errors, and for `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction` or a quoted message containing that text.

On the discover dataset those queries return transactions or mixed events. They would still be rewritten to `upsampled_count()`, summing a weight column that is absent or NULL for transactions, which gives wrong counts. The docstring claims this errs "on the side of caution", but the negated case is the opposite.

Fix: parse the query, e.g. with `event_search`, and require a positive `event.type:error` filter, with no negation and no OR containing other types.

Public entry point, caching and negated queries are untested

The tests cover only the private helpers. `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` (the function the endpoint calls, including the cache path) is never exercised, and the `self.snuba_params` built in `setUp` is unused.

Several cases are also untested:
- negated or mixed queries such as `!event.type:error`;
- top-events requests with upsampling;
- events lacking `sample_weight` in allowlisted projects.

The endpoint tests mock `options` but would not detect stale-cache behaviour.

Stray submodule gitlink committed to the repository root

The PR adds `sentry-repo` as a gitlink (`Subproject commit a5d2909…`, the base commit of this repo) with no `.gitmodules` entry. This looks like an accidental nested checkout.

It creates a dangling submodule that breaks or warns in `git submodule` operations and CI checkouts that recurse submodules, and it has nothing to do with the feature.

It should be removed from the PR.

Top-events ranking uses raw count() while plotted series use upsampled counts

For top events only `timeseries_columns` are rewritten to `upsampled_count() as count`. `selected_columns` (from `field`), `orderby` (e.g. `-count()`) and equations still reference the raw `count()`.

The top-N groups are therefore chosen by raw event count, while the values shown are weighted sums. When events carry different client sample rates, the displayed series can be out of order or omit a group that would be in the top N by upsampled count. Equations based on `count()` will also disagree with the plotted count.

upsampled_count ignores events with NULL sample_weight, so they are silently dropped

`upsampled_count` compiles to `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))`. ClickHouse `sum` skips NULL values, so any matched error without a `sample_weight` contributes 0 instead of 1. Such events include ones ingested before a project was allowlisted, ones sent without `error_sampling.client_sample_rate`, and rows from storages that never populate the column.

The comment says the schema guarantees `sample_weight`, but nothing enforces that; the allowlist is just a project-id option. Enabling a project would make historical buckets drop to near zero, and unsampled errors would vanish from charts.

Fix: aggregate `sum(ifNull(sample_weight, 1))` so unweighted events still count as one.

upsampled_count is exposed as a public user-callable function

Unlike neighbouring internal helpers, the new `SnQLFunction` is not marked `private=True`. Any user can request `upsampled_count()` directly in any discover-based query, including the transactions dataset where `sample_weight` does not exist. That produces Snuba errors.

The endpoint also bypasses all of the allowlist gating, so the function becomes part of the public query surface unintentionally.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes the get_multi result preserves the input order; dict value order is not guaranteed to match error_ids, so event data can be paired with the wrong ID (missing nodes also shift alignment).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes nodestore get_multi preserves input order

`nodestore.backend.get_multi` returns a dict keyed by node_id. Its order is not guaranteed to match `error_ids`: cached items come first, then fetched ones, and missing entries may be omitted entirely. Zipping `error_ids` with `events.values()` can therefore attach the wrong event id to each payload, or shift every id after a missing one.

Look up each payload by its generated node_id instead, e.g. `events.get(Event.generate_node_id(project_id, event_id))`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoded empty data passed to TableWidgetVisualization causes it to always render an empty table instead of displaying actual results when the feature flag is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Feature-flagged TableWidgetVisualization always renders an empty table

When `use-table-widget-visualization` is enabled, the widget renders `TableWidgetVisualization` with `columns={[]}` and hard-coded empty `tableData`. It ignores `result.data`, `result.meta`, the loading state and the field aliases.

Any org with the flag on sees empty table widgets on every dashboard, with no loading indicator. Map `result` into `TabularData` and columns before gating real users onto this flag.

true_positives.golden_comment: Validation logic incorrectly uses .get('timestamp'), which treats a timestamp of 0 as absent. It should directly check 'timestamp' in self.initial_data to ensure proper field presence detection, preventing both 'age=0' and 'timestamp' from passing mutual-exclusion validation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Mutual-exclusion check for age/timestamp uses truthiness

`validate_timestamp` checks `self.initial_data.get("age")` and `validate_age` checks `self.initial_data.get("timestamp")`. A legitimate value of 0 is falsy, so a report carrying both `timestamp` and `age: 0` passes validation even though the fields are meant to be mutually exclusive. `age` is in milliseconds, so 0 is realistic.

Nothing requires at least one of the two to be present either, despite the docstrings. Use `"age" in self.initial_data` / `"timestamp" in self.initial_data`, and add a `validate()` that requires exactly one.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The BrowserReportingCollectorEndpoint returns HttpResponse objects but the endpoint inherits from Endpoint which expects rest_framework.response.Response objects.
In BaseDetectorTypeValidator.update(), the validator incorrectly updates instance.type using validated_data.get('detector_type') instead of validated_data.get('type').

Analytics events are recorded before the feature flag check, resulting in analytics being logged for all requests, including those that return 404 due to the feature being disabled. This can lead to misleading analytics data.

false_positives.candidate:
Container lost align-items and gap during Flex migration

The removed `Container` was `styled(FlexBox)`, so it had `align-items: center` and `gap: space(1)` in addition to `justify-content: space-between`. The replacement `<Flex ref={setRef} justify="space-between">` sets only the justify.

The tabs and `TraceContextVitals` are no longer vertically centered and have no gap between them, which is a visual regression from what was meant to be a no-op refactor. Add `align="center" gap={space(1)}`.

Data migrations turned into no-ops pointing to a migration not included in this PR

Both 0917 and 0920 now just `return` and point readers to `0921_convert_org_saved_searches_to_views_rerevised.py`. That migration is not added in this PR, and the migrations lockfile is unchanged.

If 0921 does not already exist, organization-visible saved searches are never converted to GroupSearchViews. This affects every environment that has not run these migrations yet, including self-hosted. The comment would also be a dangling reference. Either include the replacement migration or confirm it exists.

Error timestamps (seconds) are compared with rrweb event timestamps (milliseconds)

`fetch_error_details` takes `timestamp` from the nodestore event payload, which is float seconds since epoch (~1.7e9). `gen_request_data` compares it against the top-level `timestamp` of replay recording events (lines 153-155). The JS SDK writes those in milliseconds (`breadcrumb.timestamp * 1000`, ~1.7e12).

With real data every error looks earlier than every breadcrumb. All errors are emitted at the start of the log instead of being interleaved chronologically, which is the main point of this change. The emitted messages also mix units (`at 1.7e9` for errors, `at 1.7e12` for breadcrumbs), which misleads the LLM.

The tests hide this because they use seconds for both. Convert the error timestamp to milliseconds (`* 1000`) before sorting and comparing, and use ms in the tests.

HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES are only hidden while a search query is entered

The memo returns `sorted` unfiltered when `searchQuery` is empty. The `!HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES.includes(attribute.name)` check only runs in the search branch.

In the default view (no search) `is_segment`, `project_id` and `received` are still shown. They disappear only once the user types something, which is inconsistent and almost certainly not intended. Filter out hidden attributes before the early return.

No remaining test exercises the application/reports+json content type

The removed `test_logs_request_data_if_option_enabled` and the old multiple-reports test were the only tests that posted with `content_type="application/reports+json"`. Every test now uses the default JSON format.

The custom `BrowserReportsJSONParser` is the content type real browsers send, and it is no longer covered. A regression in parser registration would go unnoticed. Keep at least one success-path test using that media type.

One invalid report rejects the whole batch, so valid reports are dropped and retried

The endpoint returns 422 as soon as any report in the array fails validation, for example an unlisted or new report type in the strict `ChoiceField`. Per the Reporting API, any non-2xx response marks delivery as failed, and the browser retries the entire batch.

As a result, the valid reports in that batch are never counted, and the same payload is re-sent repeatedly. Consider counting the valid reports and logging or skipping the invalid ones instead of failing the request.

Query key omits organization, allowing cached attributes to leak across orgs

The new react-query key is `['use-trace-item-attribute-keys', queryOptions]`. `queryOptions` contains item type, attribute type, project ids and datetime, but not the organization slug, while the queryFn fetches `/organizations/${organization.slug}/...`.

When switching organizations with the same page filters (e.g. `projects: []` for "My Projects" and the same period), the cached attribute keys from the previous org are served until the refetch completes.

This refactor also dropped the previous `retry: false` / `refetchOnWindowFocus: false`, so failures now retry with backoff by default. Include `organization.slug` in the key and restore the intended query options.

true_positives.golden_comment: Backup code validation is case-sensitive due to the use of indexOf(). This causes validation to fail if a user enters uppercase hex characters, as backup codes should be case-insensitive for a better user experience.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup code input not normalized for case/whitespace

Codes are generated as lowercase hex (`randomBytes(5).toString('hex')`). The input only strips dashes before an exact `indexOf` match. The same applies in disable.ts line 61.

The input placeholder is "XXXXX-XXXXX" (uppercase), and users commonly paste with leading or trailing whitespace. Either case makes a valid code fail with "Backup code is incorrect."

Apply `.trim().toLowerCase()` (and drop all non-hex characters) before comparing.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup code consumption is a non-atomic read-modify-write

The code reads the encrypted backup-code array, finds the index in memory, nulls it, and writes the whole re-encrypted blob back. Nothing makes this atomic: no transaction, no conditional update, no version check.

- Two concurrent logins with the same code both pass the `indexOf` check and both succeed, so a single-use code can be used twice.
- Two concurrent logins with different codes each null their own index on the same stale copy. The last writer wins and restores the other, already-used code to valid.

Use a conditional update (e.g. `updateMany` where `backupCodes` equals the value that was read, then fail if count is 0) or a serializable transaction.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The exported function TwoFactor handles backup codes and is in BackupCode.tsx. Inconsistent naming.
Error message mentions 'backup code login' but this is a disable endpoint, not login

Object URL for backup codes is not revoked on component unmount, leading to a potential memory leak. This can cause increased memory usage over time, especially if the component is mounted and unmounted frequently.

false_positives.candidate:
Assertion on un-awaited promise always passes; backup-code login/disable untested

`expect(page.locator(...).isChecked()).toBeTruthy()` asserts on a Promise object, which is always truthy. The PR adds a FIXME acknowledging this instead of fixing it (e.g. `await expect(locator).toBeChecked()`).

With the new flow, the dialog in this test stays open on the backup-codes screen and `onEnable` is never triggered. The broken assertion hides that.

The core new behavior (logging in with a backup code, single-use consumption, disabling 2FA with a backup code) also has no test; it is left as a TODO at line 12.

Backup code alone logs in without a password when any totpCode is sent

Line 121 only checks the password when `credentials.totpCode` is falsy (`if (user.password && !credentials.totpCode)`). The new backup-code branch at line 131 runs before the TOTP branch and never looks at `totpCode`.

So a request to the credentials provider with `email`, any non-empty `totpCode` (e.g. "1"), and one valid `backupCode` skips the password check, passes the backup-code check, and returns an authenticated user. A leaked backup code (they are offered as a downloadable txt file) is then enough to take over a CAL-password account, which defeats the purpose of a second factor.

Fix: always verify the password for CAL users regardless of `totpCode`, or at least reject requests that carry a backupCode with a totpCode and require password verification on the backup-code path.

Backup codes stored reversibly encrypted instead of hashed

Backup codes only ever need to be verified, never displayed again. Yet they are stored with `symmetricEncrypt` under the shared `CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, so anyone with DB access plus that key can recover every user's plaintext codes.

Storing a salted hash per code (and deleting the matching hash on use) is the standard approach. It would also remove the decrypt/re-encrypt round-trip on every login.

Copy button throws or falsely reports success when clipboard API unavailable

`navigator.clipboard` is undefined in non-secure contexts, e.g. a self-hosted instance served over plain http. There, `navigator.clipboard.writeText` throws a TypeError synchronously.

When the API does exist, the returned promise is not awaited, so the "Backup codes copied!" toast is shown even if the write is rejected.

Await the promise, catch errors, and only show the success toast when the write actually succeeded.

Dismissing the dialog on the backup-codes step leaves UI out of sync and step stale

After a successful enable, `onEnable()` is no longer called. It now only runs when the user clicks "Close" on the new DisplayBackupCodes step. 2FA is already enabled on the server at this point.

If the user dismisses the dialog any other way (Escape or overlay click, both handled by `onOpenChange`), then:
- `onEnable` never fires, so the parent never refreshes and the 2FA switch keeps showing "disabled".
- `resetState` never runs, so `step` stays `DisplayBackupCodes`. Reopening the modal from the (wrong) unchecked switch lands directly on the old backup codes screen.

Either call `onEnable` (or a refresh) as soon as enable succeeds, or handle `onOpenChange` on this step the same way as Close.

missing_backup_codes message points to a settings feature that doesn't exist

The message reads "No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings." This PR adds no UI or endpoint to generate or regenerate backup codes. `setup.ts` refuses to run when 2FA is already enabled, so the only path is to disable and re-enable 2FA.

This error is mainly hit on the login page by users who enabled 2FA before this change. They cannot reach settings at all, so the message gives instructions they cannot follow.

Separately, once all codes are consumed the stored array is all nulls and still truthy. Those users get "incorrect backup code" instead of this message.

tabIndex=-1 removes keyboard access to password visibility toggle

This shared `PasswordField` is used across the app. Adding `tabIndex={-1}` to the show/hide password button means keyboard-only and screen-reader users can no longer reach the toggle.

This is an accessibility regression unrelated to the backup-code feature.

`evt.destinationCalendar` is set to `null` when neither the event type nor the organizer has a destination calendar. `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)` is then a no-op, so for a collective event the other hosts' destination calendars are silently discarded. true_positives.matched_candidate:
Computed keys `[z.string().toString()]` produce a single bogus "[object Object]" field

`z.string().toString()` evaluates to the string "[object Object]". Both computed keys collapse into one property named "[object Object]", and the second definition (`z.unknown().optional()`) overwrites the first. The effective schema is `{ access_token: string }`, and zod's default strip mode then drops every other field, including expiry_date, expires_in, instance_url and scope. In sync mode the output is always just `{access_token, refresh_token: "refresh_token"}`. Consequences: Zoom computes `expiry_date = Date.now() + undefined*1000 = NaN`, which is stored as null and fails `zoomTokenSchema` next time. Office365 never updates expiry and refreshes on every call. Salesforce loses `instance_url`. Use `.passthrough()` or `.catchall()` and validate the expiry field explicitly.

Google credential key is overwritten with the safeParse wrapper object

Now `key` is the wrapper, and `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })` persists `{ success, data }` as the credential key. On the next instantiation, `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` in `googleAuth` throws. - HubSpot returns a `TokenResponseIF` and reads `.expiresIn` / `.accessToken`.
- Zoho CRM and Bigin return axios responses and read `.data.error`.

There is no try/catch, so the caller gets an unhandled 500 instead of a 400 with a useful message. That makes integration failures hard to diagnose for self-hosters. Choice of schema doesn't match where the tokens actually came from

`refreshOAuthTokens` only calls the sync endpoint when `userId` is non-null. `parseRefreshTokenResponse` switches to the minimal schema whenever sync is enabled, regardless of where the tokens came from. Two cases get a genuine provider response parsed (and stripped) with the minimal schema:
- Team credentials (userId null), whose refresh went to the real provider.
- Salesforce, which calls the provider directly and never goes through `refreshOAuthTokens`.

Those stored credentials lose required fields. The two helpers need a shared decision, for example by passing a flag or returning the source along with the response.

No tests for the new sync helpers or the webhook

The PR changes token refresh for about ten integrations and adds a credential-writing webhook, but includes no unit tests. The PR description says as much. Simple tests would have caught several of the bugs above: the `[object Object]` schema key, the safeParse wrapper being persisted as Google's key, and the Response shape mismatch in sync mode.

Outbound token-sync request carries no authentication

The request to `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` sends only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug`, with no shared secret, signature or auth header. The self-hoster's endpoint returns live third-party access tokens. To work with Cal.com it has to accept unauthenticated requests keyed by a sequential integer user ID, so anyone who can reach it can enumerate IDs and harvest every user's OAuth tokens. The inbound webhook uses a secret and encryption, but the outbound direction has neither. Send the webhook secret (or an HMAC) and expect the response to be encrypted with `CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY`.

Synced credential update doesn't clear the `invalid` flag

Adapters such as Google, Zoom and Webex mark credentials `invalid: true` on `invalid_grant`. When the parent app pushes fresh keys through this webhook, only `key` is updated, so the credential stays flagged invalid even though it now holds valid tokens. Set `invalid: false` on update.

Webhook secret compared with non-constant-time `!==`

The secret header is checked with a plain string inequality. That leaks timing information an attacker can use to guess the secret, and this endpoint can write arbitrary credentials for any user. Use `crypto.timingSafeEqual` on equal-length buffers. The handler also accepts any HTTP method; restrict it to POST.

Zoom sync uses slug "zoomvideo" instead of the app slug "zoom"

The Zoom app's slug/appId is "zoom", which is what `createOAuthAppCredential` uses and what the webhook matches against `prisma.app.slug`. The refresh call sends `appSlug=zoomvideo`, the directory name. A self-hoster implementing the sync endpoint therefore sees a slug that doesn't match the one they must send to `/api/webhook/app-credential`.

`prisma` used without being imported

The new `prisma.credential.update(...)` call references `prisma`, but this file never imports `@calcom/prisma`. It can only resolve through the dev-only `globalThis.prisma` cache, which is typed `PrismaClient | undefined` and is not set in production. In production `getClient` throws a ReferenceError, so the Salesforce integration fails for every operation.
