false_positives.candidate:
No regression test for the data race being fixed

The PR's stated purpose is to fix a data race on `entryPointAssetsCache`, but it adds no test. A small test would lock in the fix: call `GetWebAssets` from several goroutines concurrently against a fixture manifest and run it under `go test -race`. Without it, a future refactor (for example, removing the TODO'd global state, or adding another unguarded access) could reintroduce the race unnoticed.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enableSqlExpressions has inverted naming and ignores the feature flag

`enableSqlExpressions` sets `enabled := !IsEnabledGlobally(FlagSqlExpressions)`, so `enabled` is true when the flag is OFF. Both branches then return false, so the toggle is read but has no effect.

This is misleading. A future maintainer who edits one branch to "re-enable" the feature could easily get the polarity wrong and turn SQL expressions on when the flag is off, re-opening the RCE/LFI.

It also adds a needless dereference of `h.features` (a nil-features reader now panics on the SQL path).

User-facing problems:
- The `sqlExpressions` toggle is still registered and documented as enabling the feature, but it is now a silent no-op.
- The returned error says "sqlExpressions is not implemented" rather than that the feature is disabled.

Replace the function with an unconditional, clearly commented disable and a clear error message. Also update or deprecate the toggle docs.

true_positives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Existing SQL expression tests will fail against the new stub DB

The new stub `RunCommands` and `QueryFramesInto` always return "not implemented". As a result `sql.TablesList` and `expr.NewSQLCommand` now always return an error.

Existing tests still assume they succeed and were not updated or skipped in this PR:
- `pkg/expr/sql/parser_test.go` (e.g. `TestParse`, which expects `TablesList("select * from foo")` to return `foo`).
- `pkg/expr/sql_command_test.go` (`TestNewCommand`, which expects `NewSQLCommand("a", "select a from foo, bar")` to succeed).

These tests will fail CI. They should be skipped or rewritten to assert the new disabled behaviour.

false_positives.candidate:
Every SQL expression attempt now logs at Error level

With the stub DB, `RunCommands` always fails. So every SQL expression that reaches `TablesList` (e.g. via the legacy `UnmarshalSQLCommand` path) logs `logger.Error("error serializing sql", ...)`, which includes the full user-supplied SQL. `NewSQLCommand` then logs an additional Warn.

This is expected, permanent behaviour for a disabled feature, not an error condition. It creates log noise and records arbitrary user query text at error level.

Short-circuit before calling the stub, or lower the log level.

Legacy SQL expression path is not explicitly gated; relies only on the stub

The explicit disable check was added only in `ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery`. The legacy graph-building path (`buildCMDNode` -> `UnmarshalSQLCommand` -> `NewSQLCommand`) has no equivalent gate. It is blocked today only because the stub `sql.TablesList` happens to fail.

On that path users get a generic "error reading SQL command" BadRequest instead of a clear "disabled" error. The security fix also depends on the stub never being replaced with a real engine.

Add the same explicit rejection in `UnmarshalSQLCommand`/`NewSQLCommand` so both entry points are covered consistently.

No regression test for the security disable

This PR is the in-repo version of the CVE-2024-9264 fix, but it adds no test asserting that a `type: sql` expression is rejected. That should be checked both with the `sqlExpressions` toggle on and off, and through both the `ReadQuery` and `UnmarshalSQLCommand` paths.

Without such a test, a future change could silently re-enable SQL expressions and nothing would catch it.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs iterates the index cache without a lock while the watch goroutine can write to it

`bleveBackend.TotalDocs` ranges over `b.cache` without holding `cacheMu`. This PR adds a call to it in `searchSupport.init` (search.go:216), after the watch goroutine has already started at search.go:207.

That goroutine calls `handleEvent` -> `getOrCreateIndex` -> `BuildIndex`, which now writes `b.cache[key]` under `cacheMu.Lock()` (bleve.go:137-139). If a write event arrives for a resource that has no index yet, the map write can overlap with the unlocked iteration in `TotalDocs`.

Go treats concurrent map iteration and write as a fatal, unrecoverable runtime error, so this can crash the process at startup. `TotalDocs` should take `b.cacheMu.RLock()`, or the log line should run before the watcher is started.

false_negatives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.

false_positives.candidate:
Errgroup workers share and overwrite the outer `err` and `totalBatchesIndexed` variables

Inside `group.Go`, each worker assigns to the enclosing function's `err` (`_, _, err = s.build(...)`) and returns it, and also increments `totalBatchesIndexed++` without synchronization.

Before this PR, `bleveBackend.BuildIndex` held `cacheMu` for its entire duration, which effectively serialized most of the work. This PR removes that lock so builds really run in parallel with up to `initWorkers` goroutines, which widens the race window considerably.

One worker can overwrite `err` between another worker's assignment and its `return err`. A failed index build can then be reported as success, letting startup continue with a missing index, or a successful worker can return another worker's error. The `namespaced_indexed` span attribute is also racy.

Fix: use a local variable (`_, _, err := s.build(...)`) and an atomic counter.

Init failure in the constructor leaks the cancel func and background watchers

`NewResourceServer` now runs `s.Init(ctx)` and returns `nil, err` on failure without calling `s.cancel()` or `lifecycle.Stop`.

If `search.init` succeeds and `initWatcher` then fails, the search watcher has already been started: it called `WatchWriteEvents` with `context.Background()`, and its backend poller goroutine runs until the backend is stopped. Because the server is never returned, nobody can stop it. The cancelable context created for the server is also never cancelled.

Call `cancel()` and stop the lifecycle hooks on the error path.

Postgres integration test disabled instead of fixed

This PR adds an unconditional skip for postgres in `TestIntegrationWillRunInstrumentationServerWhenTargetHasNoHttpServer`, noting that it "works locally".

The PR moves resource server initialization (DB init and migrations, building indexes for every namespace, starting watchers) into the constructor, which runs during `InitializeModuleServer`. A CI failure that appears together with this change is likely related to it, for example a timeout or a connection issue at construction time.

Skipping the test removes postgres coverage of the storage-server target exactly when its startup behaviour changes. The root cause should be investigated, or at least tracked with an issue link, rather than silently skipped.

Stop() no longer causes requests to be rejected because handlers stopped checking Init

`Stop` sets `s.initErr` to "service is stopping" / "service is stopped". This was the mechanism that made subsequent gRPC calls fail, because every handler called `s.Init(ctx)` and the already-completed `sync.Once` returned `initErr`.

This PR removes the `Init` call from all handlers (Create, Update, Delete, Read, List, Watch, Search, History, Origin, IsHealthy, PutBlob, GetBlob), and nothing else reads `initErr`. After `Stop`, requests are still served against a backend whose lifecycle has been stopped and whose watch context is cancelled. `IsHealthy` also keeps reporting healthy during shutdown.

If stop semantics are still wanted, keep a cheap check of a stopped/initErr flag in the handlers (protected against the data race with `Stop`).

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Test cleanup removes IDP with literal alias "alias" instead of the created IDPs

`getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove);` points at an IDP named "alias", which does not exist. The same mistake appears again at line 425. None of the 21 IDPs created by `testCacheIDPForLogin` (`idp-alias-0`..`idp-alias-20`) are ever cleaned up.

If the realm is not re-imported, they leak into other tests. Re-running the test would also make the `create(...)` calls fail with conflicts that go unnoticed, because the responses are closed without checking status. The cleanup should use the real alias (e.g. `get("idp-alias-" + i)`).

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

false_positives.candidate:
Merging a previously read query can re-insert stale search results after a concurrent invalidation

When the cached `IdentityProviderListQuery` exists but lacks the current `searchKey`, the code proceeds in this order:
1. It reads `query` (line 222).
2. It calls `cache.invalidateObject(cacheKey)`.
3. It reads a fresh revision.
4. It builds a new query that copies all of the old query's searches (`new IdentityProviderListQuery(..., query)`).
5. It adds the result with `cache.getCurrentCounter()`.

If another transaction invalidates `cacheKey` between steps 1 and 2, the old searches are already stale. They still get merged in and stored with an up-to-date revision, so `addRevisioned` accepts them. Typical triggers are creating, removing, or relinking a login IDP.

The login cache can then keep serving outdated ID lists for other organizations: newly added brokers go missing, or brokers that became hidden or unlinked still show. This copies the pattern from `getByOrganization`, but it now affects the login page. The merge should be dropped, or the code should verify the entry was not invalidated between the read and the re-add.

Single cache entry per fetch mode accumulates one result set per organization and is rebuilt on every new org

The cache key is only realm + FetchMode, and the organization ID is used as a search key inside one `IdentityProviderListQuery`. For `ALL`/`ORG_ONLY` with an organizationId, each organization not yet seen does three things:
- triggers `invalidateObject` on the shared entry,
- copies the entire existing map of searches,
- re-adds it.

In realms with many organizations, this entry grows without bound, since it holds a set per org. It is also repeatedly invalidated and copied during normal login traffic. Any login-relevant IDP change then discards all of it at once. Consider keying the cache entry by organization (as `getByOrganization` does with `cacheKeyOrgId`), or bounding the stored searches.

Update decides login-cache invalidation using the org-aware model, which disagrees with what the cached list contains

In `update`, the 'original' IDP comes from `getById()` (line 91). That method returns `createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel(...)`, whose `isEnabled()` returns false when the linked organization is disabled, or when organizations are disabled for the realm.

The cached login ID lists, however, are filled from `idpDelegate.getForLogin(...)`. That is a raw DB query on the ENABLED/LINK_ONLY/HIDE_ON_LOGIN/BROKER_PUBLIC columns and ignores organization status.

Example: an org is disabled and one of its public, enabled IDPs is in the cached list. An admin then sets that IDP to hideOnLogin=true, linkOnly=true, or removes BROKER_PUBLIC. `getLoginPredicate().test(original)` is false because the wrapped `isEnabled()` is false. `test(updated)` is also false. So `registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate` returns early (line 405) and nothing is invalidated.

The stale ID stays in the cached list. Once the org is re-enabled, `getForLogin` keeps returning it. `OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean` only re-checks `isEnabled()`, so a hidden, link-only, or non-public broker appears on the login page until some other change invalidates the cache.

Fix: evaluate the original with the raw model (e.g. `idpDelegate.getById(...)`), so the comparison uses the same view as the cached query.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract `order()` breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations

`int order()` is added to the public `CryptoProvider` SPI as an abstract method. Any external or custom implementation no longer compiles.

Binaries compiled against the previous `keycloak-common` are worse: when such a provider is discovered, `Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order)` in `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` throws `AbstractMethodError` during the sort. That aborts crypto initialization entirely, even if a valid built-in provider is also present.

A `default int order() { return 0; }` (or similar) would keep the SPI backward compatible while still letting the built-in providers take precedence.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)

Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

false_positives.candidate:
ES384/ES512 tests use a P-256 key, so long-form DER lengths are never tested and only a self-roundtrip is checked

The test builds one key pair with `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()`, which defaults to P-256, and reuses it for ES256, ES384 and ES512. With a P-256 key, r and s are at most 33 bytes and the DER SEQUENCE is under 128 bytes. So the long-form length paths in the new `ASN1Encoder.writeLength` and `ASN1Decoder.readLength` (needed for P-521/ES512, where the sequence is about 136-139 bytes) are never executed. The 48- and 66-byte component sizes are only checked as zero padding of 32-byte values.

The test also compares only the output of the hand-written decoder against itself after a round trip through the hand-written encoder. A symmetric encoding bug would pass. It never checks the re-encoded DER with `Signature.verify`, and never compares against a reference implementation such as BC.

Suggested fix: generate a key on the matching curve (secp256r1/secp384r1/secp521r1) for each algorithm, and assert that `signature.verify(asn1Des)` succeeds.

Multiple equal-order crypto providers are now silently resolved by classpath order

`detectProvider` used to throw when more than one `CryptoProvider` was found. It now sorts by `order()` and takes the first. `DefaultCryptoProvider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider` and `FIPS1402Provider` all return 200, so a tie between them is broken only by the stable sort, i.e. by `ServiceLoader`/classpath order. The ignored providers are logged at DEBUG only.

Consequence: a deployment that relies on `CryptoIntegration.init` (not `setProvider`) and has both the FIPS and the default crypto jars on the classpath now silently picks one at random instead of failing. It may run in non-FIPS mode without any visible warning.

All discovered providers are also instantiated before sorting. The constructors of `FIPS1402Provider` and `DefaultCryptoProvider` change JVM-global state: they insert BCFIPS/BCJSSE/KeycloakFipsSecurityProvider at positions 1-3, add BC, and rewrite `ssl.KeyManagerFactory.algorithm`. A provider that loses the tie still leaves those changes behind. Before this PR startup aborted in that case.

Suggested fix: keep the hard failure (or at least WARN) when the two highest-ranked providers have the same `order()`, and only drop lower-ranked ones.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client removal no longer cleans up permission data; V2 has no replacement

The removal listener now runs only when V1 `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ` is enabled. Previously it always cleaned up V1 client/role/group permission objects. If V1 permissions were created and the feature later disabled, deleting clients, roles or groups now leaves orphaned resources and policies.

Under V2, nothing removes the per-client resource and permissions created by `getOrCreateResource` when a client is deleted. Stale permissions referencing non-existent clients accumulate in the admin-permissions resource server.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getClientsWithPermission returns the string 'Clients' instead of client ids

`resourceStore.findByType(server, "Clients", ...)` only matches resources whose type is 'Clients'. In the V2 schema that is just the all-clients resource created by `init()`; per-client resources are created by `getOrCreateResource` without a type.

The method therefore never returns real client ids. When an all-clients permission grants the scope, it returns `{"Clients"}` (the resource name), which callers will treat as a client id. Per-client grants are ignored entirely.

It should iterate per-client resources (or the policies attached to them) and return the client ids those resource names represent.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
NPE when the 'Clients' all-resource is missing

When no per-client resource exists, `hasPermission(ClientModel, String)` falls back to `getResourceTypeResource(...)`. That call returns null in two cases: `supportsAuthorizationSchema` is false (for example, realm admin permissions were disabled but the admin-permissions client still exists), or the 'Clients' resource was never created (realms initialized before this change, since `init()` returns early when the client exists).

The null is then passed directly to `getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource)` and later to `resource.getScopes()`, which throws a NullPointerException. Every client admin endpoint called by an admin without manage-clients would return 500.

The sibling `hasPermission(String)` null-checks the resource; this branch should do the same and return false.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.

false_positives.candidate:
Any per-client permission suppresses all-clients grants for every other scope

If a resource exists for the client, only that resource is evaluated. Per-client resources are created without a type, and all-clients permissions are attached to the 'Clients' resource, so the policy evaluator never picks up the all-clients permissions for that client.

Example: an admin has an all-clients MANAGE permission and a per-client permission granting only MAP_ROLES on client X. `canManage(X)` then returns false, even though the admin can manage every other client.

The fallback should be per scope: when the specific resource yields no decision for the requested scope, also evaluate the all-clients resource. Otherwise only deny on the same scope should override.

Javadoc for void require* methods says 'Returns true'

The new Javadoc on `requireView()` says "Returns {@code true} if {@link #canView()} returns {@code true}", and `requireViewClientScopes()` has the same wording. Both methods are void and throw ForbiddenException on failure.

The docs should match the other require* methods: "Throws ForbiddenException if canView()/canViewClientScopes() returns false".

Per-client deny on VIEW is bypassed by the all-clients VIEW check

`canView(ClientModel)` first calls `canView()`. That evaluates only the all-clients 'Clients' resource and returns true as soon as an all-clients VIEW permission grants. The client-specific resource is never consulted.

As a result, a negative per-client VIEW permission (all clients viewable except X) has no effect. `requireView(X)` succeeds, and `ClientsResource.getClients` (which computes `canView()` once) lists every client.

The user resource type tests (`testViewUserPermission`, `testImpersonatePermission`) establish that a resource-specific permission overrides the all-resource one, so client semantics are inconsistent. This is also untested.

Realms already initialized never receive the new Clients resource and scopes

`init()` returns early when the admin-permissions client already exists. Realms that enabled admin permissions before this change never get:
- the 'Clients' all-resource;
- the new `configure`, `map-roles-client-scope` and `map-roles-composite` scopes.

For those realms, creating a client permission fails ("Scope [configure] does not exist" / "No scopes found."). Evaluation also hits the null all-clients resource path in `ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission`.

The schema should be reconciled for existing clients, adding missing scopes and resource-type resources.

Repeated full policy evaluations per client in listings

Each `hasPermission` call evaluates the resource with all of its scopes and then checks a single scope. In the fallback path it also loads all policies of the 'Clients' resource just to test emptiness.

`canView(c)` alone triggers up to 4 evaluations: `canView()`, MANAGE via `canConfigure`, CONFIGURE, and VIEW. `getAccess(c)` repeats `canView`, `canManage` and `canConfigure`. Listing N clients therefore performs roughly 10+ evaluations and extra policy queries per client.

The granted scopes from one evaluation could be computed once per client (and the all-clients result once per request) and reused.

Test rotates the secret of the client used by the injected admin client and leaves other mutations unrestored

`testConfigureOnlyOneClient` calls `generateNewSecret()` and `invalidateRotatedSecret()` on `myclient`. That is the confidential client (secret "mysecret") the `realmAdminClient` authenticates with, and nothing restores the secret. Any later re-authentication or token refresh by `realmAdminClient` in this class will fail with 401, making results order-dependent.

Other tests have the same problem with no cleanup registered:
- `testManageOnlyOneClient` renames `myclient` and moves a default client scope to optional;
- `testMapRolesAndCompositesOnlyOneClient` creates client roles and maps one to `myadmin`.

These changes should be registered via `realm.cleanup()` or done on a dedicated client.

canExchangeTo now throws UnsupportedOperationException, breaking token exchange under V2

Before this PR, `MgmtPermissionsV2.clients()` returned the V1 `ClientPermissions`. It now returns `ClientPermissionsV2`, whose `canExchangeTo` throws `UnsupportedOperationException`.

The token exchange provider calls `AdminPermissions.management(session, realm).clients().canExchangeTo(...)` when exchanging to another client. With the V2 feature enabled, such requests will fail with a 500 instead of an access-denied response.

The unused `getEvaluationContext` helper and `TOKEN_EXCHANGE` import suggest this was meant to be implemented. At minimum it should return false or delegate rather than throw.

Similarly, `isPermissionsEnabled`/`setPermissionsEnabled` now throw. Those are reached from the `/clients/{id}/management/permissions` endpoints, which will return 500.

canView() ignores all-clients MANAGE, inconsistent with canView(ClientScopeModel)

`canView()` only checks the manage-clients/view-clients roles and the all-clients VIEW scope.

An admin granted all-clients MANAGE gets:
- `canManage()` and `canManageClientScopes()` true;
- `canView(ClientScopeModel)` true, since it explicitly accepts MANAGE;
- `canView()`, and therefore `canViewClientScopes()`, `requireView()` and `requireViewClientScopes()`, false.

Such an admin can modify things (for example realm default client scopes) that the view-guarded endpoints refuse to show them. Manage should imply view here, as it does in `canView(ClientScopeModel)` and via `canConfigure` in `canView(ClientModel)`.

getResourceName has no CLIENTS branch, so client permission resources render with null names

`getResourceName` maps USERS resources to "All users" or the username. For the new CLIENTS type it falls through to `resource.getDisplayName()`. Neither per-client resources (created via `resourceStore.create(...)`) nor the 'Clients' all-resource (created in `init()`) have a display name, so this returns null.

Permission resource listings for client permissions will show empty names instead of "All clients" or the client's clientId.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Incorrect method call for exit codes. The picocli.exit() method calls System.exit() directly, which is problematic:
Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance

false_positives.candidate:
Feature-disabled test checks neither the new exit code nor the `check` subcommand

`testFeatureNotEnabled` only asserts the error text for the `metadata` subcommand. The PR's main contract change is the new exit code `FEATURE_DISABLED = 4` (and the move of `RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE` from 4 to 3), and scripts are told to rely on these exit codes.

No test asserts that a disabled feature yields exit code 4, that `check` is also gated, or that an incompatible result now returns 3. A regression in the exit codes would go unnoticed. Add `assertEquals(CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED, result.exitCode())` for both subcommands, and assert 3 in `testWrongVersions`.

Hard-coded `--features=rolling-updates` in the command template can clobber the user's real feature set

The `updatecompatibility` macro now appends `--features=rolling-updates` to every documented `update-compatibility` invocation. The same guide tells users to pass exactly the options used by `start`.

Users who already run with `--features=<their list>` will now pass a second `--features` value that replaces their list. The metadata/check then runs with a different feature set than the real deployment, or the duplicate option causes a CLI error. Users need to add `rolling-updates` to their existing list, not override it.

Separately, `features` is a build-time option. With an optimized (`--optimized`) image, passing it at runtime does not take effect. The commands will then exit with code 4 unless the image was rebuilt with the feature, which is why `Dockerfile-custom-image` had to be changed. Neither point is documented.

New feature changes `--features` help output but approved help snapshots are not updated

Adding `ROLLING_UPDATES` adds `rolling-updates[:v1]` to the 'Possible values' list that the `--features` option prints in CLI help. That list is checked by the approval-based help tests (`HelpCommandDistTest.*.approved.txt` for start, start-dev, build, export, import, update-compatibility, etc.). None of those snapshot files are part of this PR, so the help tests are likely to fail once this merges. Regenerate and commit the approved help files together with the new feature.

Operator doc says the Operator will fail without `rolling-updates`, but nothing enforces this

The new CAUTION block says the `rolling-updates` feature must be enabled or 'the Keycloak Operator will fail'. This PR adds no Operator code that checks the feature. The existing `Recreate` strategy behaves the same whether or not the feature is on.

The default `<not set>` strategy also clearly works without the feature: `UpgradeTest` runs the `null` strategy case without enabling it. The statement is therefore inaccurate at this commit. Readers will also be confused about whether the feature is needed when they don't set `update.strategy`.

Either add Operator-side validation that reports a clear status error, or reword the doc to say exactly when the feature is needed and what happens without it.

true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.

canManage() is granted by the VIEW scope on all groups

`GroupPermissionsV2.canManage()` returns `hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)`. This looks copied from `canView()`. The effect is that an admin with only a read-only "view all groups" permission passes `requireManage()`.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns resource IDs and looks up resources by the wrong key

The callback passes `groupResource.getId()` (the authz resource UUID) to `hasPermission`. That method calls `resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId)`, so a resource ID is used as a name and never matches. Evaluation always falls back to the all-groups resource.

The callback then adds `groupResource.getId()` to the result. Callers treat the result as group IDs: `UsersResource`/`BruteForceUsersResource` put it in the `UserModel.GROUPS` session attribute, and `getUsersCount(realm, groupIds)` uses it.

In addition, `AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource` never calls `setType`, so `findByType(server, "Groups")` only returns the all-groups resource named "Groups". Per-group resources are never iterated.

- With an all-groups VIEW_MEMBERS permission, the set contains the "Groups" resource UUID. The user query is restricted to a non-existent group and returns no users.
- With only per-group permissions, the set is empty. The DB query is unfiltered and users are filtered in memory after pagination, so pages come back short or incomplete.

Any per-group permission hides all-groups grants for other scopes on that group

`hasPermission` falls back to the all-groups resource only when no per-group resource exists. Once any permission references a group (for example VIEW_MEMBERS on `topGroup`), that group's resource exists and only it is evaluated.

Per-group resources are created without a type, so the "Groups"-typed all-groups permissions are not included in that evaluation. As a result, an admin with "manage all groups" who is also given "view-members on topGroup" can no longer manage, view, or map roles on `topGroup`.

This also makes `canView()`/`canManage()` (all-groups) and `canView(group)`/`canManage(group)` disagree for the same group. The evaluation should combine the per-group result with the all-groups resource for scopes the per-group permissions do not decide.

Per-group resources are created by `getOrCreateResource` with the group id as name and no display name. The "Groups" type resource also has no display name. For group permissions this method therefore returns `resource.getDisplayName()`, which is null.

Resource names shown for group permissions in the admin API/UI will be null or meaningless instead of "All groups" or the group name/path.

`AdminPermissionsSchema.getResourceTypeResource(...)` can return null. This happens when the schema is not supported for the current context, or when the "Groups" resource was never created. The result is passed straight into `policyStore.findByResource(server, resource)` and later `resource.getScopes()` with no null check.

`GroupPermissionEvaluator` is reachable from `AdminPermissionEvaluator`, which custom admin REST extensions (`AdminRealmResourceProvider`) receive. Those extensions will fail to compile or link after upgrade.

a

true_positives.golden_comment: In isAccessTokenId, the substring for the grant shortcut and the equality check look inverted: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4–5 (substring(4,6)), and a match should return true (combined with UUID check), not false.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isAccessTokenId matcher never checks the grant shortcut (inverted condition, wrong offset)

The grant shortcut is the last 2 characters of the 6-character prefix, at `substring(4, 6)`. The matcher reads `items[0].substring(3, 5)`, which for `onrtac` is `ta`. It also returns `false` when the value *equals* the expected shortcut, so the condition is inverted.

With the current offset the comparison never matches, so the check is a no-op and the matcher passes any `xxxxxx:<uuid>` ID. If someone fixes only the offset, every correct token will fail.

As a result, `expectCodeToToken`, `expectRefresh`, `expectDeviceCodeToToken` and `expectAuthReqIdToToken` do not verify that the right grant type is encoded. A grant that wrongly encodes `na` would go unnoticed. A prefix shorter than 5 characters would also throw `StringIndexOutOfBoundsException` instead of failing the match.

true_positives.golden_comment: Javadoc mentions "usually like 3-letters shortcut" but some implementations use 2-letter shortcuts ("ac", "cc", "rt", "te", "pc", "ci", "ro"). Consider updating documentation to reflect actual usage pattern.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Javadoc says 'usually 3-letter' shortcut, but the default encoder requires exactly 2 characters

The contract tells implementers the shortcut is "usually like 3-letters". `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider` assumes every shortcut is exactly 2 characters: `getTokenContextFromTokenId` rejects any prefix whose length is not 6 and slices fixed 2-character segments.

A custom grant that follows the Javadoc and returns a 3-letter shortcut will issue access tokens (`onrtabc:...`) that the same provider cannot decode; it throws `IllegalArgumentException`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Catching generic RuntimeException is too broad. The implementation throws IllegalArgumentException specifically - catch that instead for more precise testing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
testIncorrectGrantType passes only because of an NPE from the null sessionFactory

Access token `jti` format change is user-visible but undocumented

The access token `jti`, and the `token_id` detail on events such as `CODE_TO_TOKEN` and `REFRESH_TOKEN`, change from a plain UUID to `xxxxxx:<uuid>`, which is 43 characters and contains a colon.

Resource servers, event listeners and audit pipelines that validate or store `jti` as a UUID, or in a 36-character column, will break after upgrade.

The PR adds no upgrade or release note for this observable contract change. One should be added.

The grant type is put into the `ClientSessionContext` in only a few places: `OAuth2GrantTypeBase.createTokenResponse`, ROPC, PreAuthorizedCode, refresh and standard token exchange.

`ClientCredentialsGrantType` is not modified. It builds its response directly with `tokenManager.responseBuilder(...).generateAccessToken()` rather than through `createTokenResponse`, so `Constants.GRANT_TYPE` is never set. Every client-credentials access token is therefore encoded with grant shortcut `na`, even though the `cc` shortcut is defined here and the unit test uses `trltcc` as an example.

The UMA permission grant (`pg`) and legacy/V1 token exchange flows have the same problem.

Future consumers (#37117, introspection optimizations) will get wrong context for these tokens. The broken `isAccessTokenId` matcher, and the fact that `expectClientLogin` does not assert `TOKEN_ID`, mean no test catches this.

Fix: set `clientSessionCtx.setAttribute(Constants.GRANT_TYPE, context.getGrantType())` in `ClientCredentialsGrantType`, and likewise for the other flows that bypass `createTokenResponse`.

The runtime impact is worse. A custom factory compiled against the old SPI will throw `AbstractMethodError` when `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit` calls `gtf.getShortcut()` for every registered grant factory. That exception aborts `postInit` and prevents Keycloak from starting.

A factory that returns `null` causes `ConcurrentHashMap.put(null, ...)` to throw NPE in the same place.

The public `Context(Context)` copy constructor is deleted from this public SPI class without any mention in the description. Extensions that wrap or clone a grant context will no longer compile.

This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns resource IDs and looks up resources by the wrong key

The callback passes `groupResource.getId()` (the authz resource UUID) to `hasPermission`. That method calls `resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId)`, so a resource ID is used as a name and never matches. Evaluation always falls back to the all-groups resource.

The callback then adds `groupResource.getId()` to the result. Callers treat the result as group IDs: `UsersResource`/`BruteForceUsersResource` put it in the `UserModel.GROUPS` session attribute, and `getUsersCount(realm, groupIds)` uses it.

In addition, `AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource` never calls `setType`, so `findByType(server, "Groups")` only returns the all-groups resource named "Groups". Per-group resources are never iterated.

Consequences:
- With an all-groups VIEW_MEMBERS permission, the set contains the "Groups" resource UUID. The user query is restricted to a non-existent group and returns no users.
- With only per-group permissions, the set is empty. The DB query is unfiltered and users are filtered in memory after pagination, so pages come back short or incomplete.
- `/users/count` returns wrong counts in both cases.

The method should iterate per-group resources and return `resource.getName()` (the group id). The all-groups case needs its own handling.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the exact same bug as the golden comment: `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission` passes `groupResource.getId()` to `hasPermission` (which expects a resource name/group ID) and adds the resource ID to the returned set instead of the group ID (`resource.getName()`), causing broken permission evaluation and incorrect filtering in `UserModel.GROUPS` and `getUsersCount`.

false_positives.candidate:
NPE when the all-groups "Groups" resource does not exist

`AdminPermissionsSchema.getResourceTypeResource(...)` can return null. This happens when the schema is not supported for the current context, or when the "Groups" resource was never created. The result is passed straight into `policyStore.findByResource(server, resource)` and later `resource.getScopes()` with no null check.

`AdminPermissionsSchema.init` returns early if the admin-permissions client already exists. Realms that enabled admin permissions before this change therefore have no "Groups" resource and none of the new `manage-members`/`view-members`/`manage-membership` scopes.

For such realms, any admin without the `view-users`/`manage-users` roles who lists or reads groups goes through `canView(group)` and hits this path, which fails with a 500. Creating group permissions there also fails with "No scopes found".

Add a null guard here, and either add a migration or create the missing schema resources and scopes for existing admin-permissions clients.

Any per-group permission hides all-groups grants for other scopes on that group

`hasPermission` falls back to the all-groups resource only when no per-group resource exists. Once any permission references a group (for example VIEW_MEMBERS on `topGroup`), that group's resource exists and only it is evaluated.

Per-group resources are created without a type, so the "Groups"-typed all-groups permissions are not included in that evaluation. As a result, an admin with "manage all groups" who is also given "view-members on topGroup" can no longer manage, view, or map roles on `topGroup`.

This also makes `canView()`/`canManage()` (all-groups) and `canView(group)`/`canManage(group)` disagree for the same group. The evaluation should combine the per-group result with the all-groups resource for scopes the per-group permissions do not decide.

requireManageMembers Javadoc references the wrong method

The Javadoc for `requireManageMembers(GroupModel)` says it throws ForbiddenException if `canManageMembership(GroupModel)` returns false. The implementations actually check `canManageMembers(GroupModel)`, which is a different scope (MANAGE_MEMBERS vs MANAGE_MEMBERSHIP). It looks copy-pasted from `requireManageMembership` and will mislead callers.

Separately, `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission` documents its return as a "Stream" while it returns a Set.

Public evaluator interface methods renamed/removed without deprecation

`GroupPermissionEvaluator.getGroupsWithViewPermission()` is renamed to `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()`, and `getGroupsWithViewPermission(GroupModel)` is removed. `ModelToRepresentation.searchGroupModelsByAttributes` is also removed.

`GroupPermissionEvaluator` is reachable from `AdminPermissionEvaluator`, which custom admin REST extensions (`AdminRealmResourceProvider`) receive. Those extensions will fail to compile or link after upgrade.

Consider keeping the old method as a deprecated default that delegates to the new one.

Groups resource type not handled in getResourceName

The new GROUPS resource type is added, but `getResourceName` still only maps USERS resources to human-readable names ("All users" or the username).

Per-group resources are created by `getOrCreateResource` with the group id as name and no display name. The "Groups" type resource also has no display name. For group permissions this method therefore returns `resource.getDisplayName()`, which is null.

Resource names shown for group permissions in the admin API/UI will be null or meaningless instead of "All groups" or the group name/path.

testManageGroupMembership does not verify that the group-level permission is required

The test grants all-users MANAGE_GROUP_MEMBERSHIP and per-group MANAGE_MEMBERSHIP together, then only asserts that the join succeeds.

The initial negative check uses the non-existent group "no-such", so it only exercises the user-level check. Nothing asserts that the join to `topGroup` is forbidden when the group's MANAGE_MEMBERSHIP permission is absent, so a regression in `GroupPermissionsV2.canManageMembership` would go unnoticed.

The suite also has no case for all-groups VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS on user listing or count, which would expose the `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission` bug.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract `order()` breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations

`int order()` is added to the public `CryptoProvider` SPI as an abstract method. Any external or custom implementation no longer compiles.

Binaries compiled against the previous `keycloak-common` are worse: when such a provider is discovered, `Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order)` in `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` throws `AbstractMethodError` during the sort. That aborts crypto initialization entirely, even if a valid built-in provider is also present.

A `default int order() { return 0; }` (or similar) would keep the SPI backward compatible while still letting the built-in providers take precedence.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the exact same problem as the golden comment: adding an abstract `order()` method to `CryptoProvider` breaks backward compatibility with existing implementations.

false_positives.candidate:
Multiple equal-order crypto providers are now silently resolved by classpath order

`detectProvider` used to throw when more than one `CryptoProvider` was found. It now sorts by `order()` and takes the first. `DefaultCryptoProvider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider` and `FIPS1402Provider` all return 200, so a tie between them is broken only by the stable sort, i.e. by `ServiceLoader`/classpath order. The ignored providers are logged at DEBUG only.

Consequence: a deployment that relies on `CryptoIntegration.init` (not `setProvider`) and has both the FIPS and the default crypto jars on the classpath now silently picks one at random instead of failing. It may run in non-FIPS mode without any visible warning.

All discovered providers are also instantiated before sorting. The constructors of `FIPS1402Provider` and `DefaultCryptoProvider` change JVM-global state: they insert BCFIPS/BCJSSE/KeycloakFipsSecurityProvider at positions 1-3, add BC, and rewrite `ssl.KeyManagerFactory.algorithm`. A provider that loses the tie still leaves those changes behind. Before this PR startup aborted in that case.

Suggested fix: keep the hard failure (or at least WARN) when the two highest-ranked providers have the same `order()`, and only drop lower-ranked ones.

ES384/ES512 tests use a P-256 key, so long-form DER lengths are never tested and only a self-roundtrip is checked

The test builds one key pair with `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()`, which defaults to P-256, and reuses it for ES256, ES384 and ES512. With a P-256 key, r and s are at most 33 bytes and the DER SEQUENCE is under 128 bytes. So the long-form length paths in the new `ASN1Encoder.writeLength` and `ASN1Decoder.readLength` (needed for P-521/ES512, where the sequence is about 136-139 bytes) are never executed. The 48- and 66-byte component sizes are only checked as zero padding of 32-byte values.

The test also compares only the output of the hand-written decoder against itself after a round trip through the hand-written encoder. A symmetric encoding bug would pass. It never checks the re-encoded DER with `Signature.verify`, and never compares against a reference implementation such as BC.

Suggested fix: generate a key on the matching curve (secp256r1/secp384r1/secp521r1) for each algorithm, and assert that `signature.verify(asn1Des)` succeeds.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)

Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

true_positives.golden_comment: The reader thread isn’t waited for; flipping deletedAll to true and asserting immediately can race and miss exceptions added just after the flag change, making this test flaky.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reader thread is never joined, so its exceptions can be missed

The test sets `deletedAll` to true and then asserts on `caughtExceptions` right away, without joining the reader thread. At that moment the reader may still be inside a `groups()` request that overlapped the last deletions. An exception from that request is added to the list after the assertion has already passed, so a regression can go undetected. Nothing guarantees the reader issued any request during the deletion window either, so the test may pass without exercising the race at all. Keep a reference to the thread, `join()` it after setting the flag, and ideally check that at least one read overlapped the deletions.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same concurrency issue: the reader thread is not waited for (joined) after setting `deletedAll` to true, leading to a race condition where exceptions thrown by the reader thread after the assertion are missed.

false_positives.candidate:
Same NPE remains in the paginated getSubGroupsStream overloads

The fix null-guards only `getSubGroupsCount()`. The three paginated `getSubGroupsStream(...)` overloads (lines 256, 262, 268) still call `modelSupplier.get().getSubGroupsStream(...)` directly. `modelSupplier.get()` returns null when the group has been deleted in the database but the cached adapter is still in use. That is exactly the concurrent-deletion race this PR targets. Listing or paginating subgroups of a group deleted by another request will still throw a NullPointerException and return HTTP 500. These call sites should get the same null handling, e.g. return `Stream.empty()` when the model is null.

Background thread loops forever if a deletion throws

`deletedAll.set(true)` runs only after every `remove()` call succeeds. If any deletion throws (e.g. a 500 or a 404), the flag is never set. The non-daemon reader thread then keeps calling the admin API in a tight loop indefinitely. It leaks into later tests and can keep the JVM from exiting. Put the deletion loop in try/finally so the flag is always set, and make the thread a daemon or join it.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Returning null from getSubGroupsCount() violates the GroupModel contract (Javadoc says it never returns null) and may lead to NPEs in callers that expect a non-null count.

true_positives.golden_comment: In UsernameForm.authenticate(), isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() is called without passing the required UserModel parameter.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Call to non-existent no-arg isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() breaks compilation

`UsernameForm.authenticate` calls `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` with no arguments. The only method added in the superclass `UsernamePasswordForm` is `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)`, and no no-arg overload exists anywhere in the hierarchy. The services module will not compile, so neither the fix nor the new tests can run. The call should pass the current user, e.g. `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: `UsernameForm.authenticate()` calls `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` without the required `UserModel` argument.

true_positives.golden_comment: With isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user) requiring user != null, authenticate(...) will not call webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context) on the initial login page where context.getUser() is still null, so conditional passkey UI will not be set up for first-time passkey login. Consider whether this should also be enabled when no user has been selected yet so ID-less passkey authentication on the initial login form continues to work.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isConditionalPasskeysEnabled requires user != null, disabling passkeys on normal login and enabling them for every re-auth

The new helper returns `webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled() && user != null`. Before this PR, the conditional UI was filled only when no user was selected yet (the normal identity-first login). It is used in `authenticate()` (line 115) and in `challenge(context, error, field)` (line 137), and with this condition:
(1) On a fresh login where `context.getUser()` is null, `fillContextForm` is never called. The webauthn challenge and conditional UI are no longer rendered, so passkey login is broken for all first-time and logged-out logins.
(2) During re-authentication it returns true for any identified user, so the passkey UI is shown even to users with no passkey credential.
The intended condition is `user == null || user.credentialManager().isConfiguredFor(webauthnAuth.getCredentialType())`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled` requires `user != null`, which causes `fillContextForm` not to be called during the initial login when `context.getUser()` is null, thereby breaking conditional passkey UI for first-time/initial login.

false_positives.candidate:
Re-auth test for user without passkey disables passkeys realm-wide, so the per-user check is never tested

`reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey` sets `setWebAuthnPolicyPasskeysEnabled(Boolean.FALSE)` for the whole realm. The webauthn form is therefore absent simply because the feature is off, not because the user lacks a passkey. Yet the inline comment at line 304 says passkeys are unavailable "as this user does not have passkey".

The important case is never exercised: passkeys enabled in the realm, and a user without a passkey credential re-authenticating with prompt=login. That case is exactly where the `user != null` logic in `UsernamePasswordForm.isConditionalPasskeysEnabled` misbehaves. The test should keep passkeys enabled and assert the webauthn form is absent for test-user@localhost.

true_positives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Inconsistent metric tag key: 'shards' vs 'shard'

`spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` is tagged with `{"shards": shard_tag}`. `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` use `{"shard": shard_tag}` for the same value. Dashboards that group or filter these flusher metrics by one key will silently miss the other metric.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the exact same inconsistency between the 'shard' and 'shards' metric tag keys across the same specific metrics, and notes the same impact on dashboard filtering/grouping.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Added time.sleep(0.1) is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched

The test calls `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)` at the start, so the new `time.sleep(0.1)` does nothing. The comment says it gives the flusher threads time to process the drift change, but it doesn't. The test still races: `join()` sets `stopped=True` and the flusher thread may exit before it ever observes the new drift, which makes the test flaky. A real wait (e.g. the original `sleep` saved before patching, or polling until `messages` is non-empty) is needed.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: `time.sleep` is monkeypatched to be a no-op, so calling `time.sleep(0.1)` later in the test does not actually wait as intended.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Hung flusher processes are no longer killed before a replacement is spawned

The old code called `self.process.kill()` unconditionally. The new code only kills when `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` is true. Processes come from `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process`, which builds `SpawnProcess`. `SpawnProcess` subclasses `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess`, not `multiprocessing.Process` (that is `context.Process`), so the check is always False in production.

When a process is flagged as a `hang`, the still-alive old process is left running and a second process is started for the same shards. Both share the same `stopped`, `current_drift`, `healthy_since` and `backpressure_since` Values. Consequences:
- Two processes can call `flush_segments` on the same shards concurrently and produce duplicate segments to buffered-segments.
- The stale process can keep refreshing `healthy_since`, masking the new one's health.
- Up to MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS orphan processes can leak.

The same broken check at line 346 means `terminate()` in `join()` never runs either. Use `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess` (or check for not being a `threading.Thread`) instead.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: flusher processes are created via `multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process` (resulting in `SpawnProcess`), which does not subclass `multiprocessing.Process`, causing the `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` check to always evaluate to False and preventing hung processes from being killed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Added time.sleep(0.1) is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched

The test calls `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)` at the start, so the new `time.sleep(0.1)` does nothing. The comment says it gives the flusher threads time to process the drift change, but it doesn't. The test still races: `join()` sets `stopped=True` and the flusher thread may exit before it ever observes the new drift, which makes the test flaky. A real wait (e.g. the original `sleep` saved before patching, or polling until `messages` is non-empty) is needed.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same issue: `time.sleep` was monkeypatched earlier in the test, making the added `time.sleep(0.1)` a no-op and failing to give the flusher thread time to process, requiring the original sleep or an alternative synchronization method.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() breaks out of the loop on deadline and skips terminating the remaining processes

In `join()`, once the deadline has passed, `if remaining_time <= 0: break` exits the loop entirely. Every process after that point never reaches the `process.terminate()` call. Before this change, terminate was always attempted after the wait.

With several flusher processes, a timed-out join (e.g. during rebalancing) leaves the later processes running unsupervised. They can keep flushing shards that may now belong to another consumer. A stuck process would never exit, because it is only stopped via the `stopped` flag.

The deadline check should only skip the waiting, not the termination.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same bug: breaking out of the loop when the deadline expires skips calling terminate() on the remaining flusher processes, leaving them running.

false_positives.candidate:
Cluster-wide Redis memory info is queried once per flusher buffer on every submit

`get_memory_info()` reports memory for the whole Redis cluster, not for a shard. The new loop calls it once per per-process buffer, so every `submit()` issues N times as many INFO calls to every cluster node.

The used/available ratio comes out the same only because both sums are multiplied by N. The extra calls are pure overhead on the consumer's main thread, which this PR is trying to keep minimal.

`record_stored_segments` is likewise split into N separate pipelines. Query memory info once (e.g. from a single buffer) instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes the get_multi result preserves the input order; dict value order is not guaranteed to match error_ids, so event data can be paired with the wrong ID (missing nodes also shift alignment).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes nodestore get_multi preserves input order

`nodestore.backend.get_multi` returns a dict keyed by node_id. Its order is not guaranteed to match `error_ids`: cached items come first, then fetched ones, and missing entries may be omitted entirely. Zipping `error_ids` with `events.values()` can therefore attach the wrong event id to each payload, or shift every id after a missing one.

Look up each payload by its generated node_id instead, e.g. `events.get(Event.generate_node_id(project_id, event_id))`.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the exact same bug as the golden comment: using `zip(error_ids, events.values())` wrongly assumes `get_multi` preserves input order and handles missing items without shifting alignment, leading to mismatched IDs and event payloads.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoded empty data passed to TableWidgetVisualization causes it to always render an empty table instead of displaying actual results when the feature flag is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Feature-flagged TableWidgetVisualization always renders an empty table

When `use-table-widget-visualization` is enabled, the widget renders `TableWidgetVisualization` with `columns={[]}` and hard-coded empty `tableData`. It ignores `result.data`, `result.meta`, the loading state and the field aliases.

Any org with the flag on sees empty table widgets on every dashboard, with no loading indicator. Map `result` into `TabularData` and columns before gating real users onto this flag.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: when the feature flag is enabled, TableWidgetVisualization is passed hardcoded empty data/columns instead of actual results, causing it to always render an empty table.

true_positives.golden_comment: Validation logic incorrectly uses .get('timestamp'), which treats a timestamp of 0 as absent. It should directly check 'timestamp' in self.initial_data to ensure proper field presence detection, preventing both 'age=0' and 'timestamp' from passing mutual-exclusion validation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Mutual-exclusion check for age/timestamp uses truthiness

`validate_timestamp` checks `self.initial_data.get("age")` and `validate_age` checks `self.initial_data.get("timestamp")`. A legitimate value of 0 is falsy, so a report carrying both `timestamp` and `age: 0` passes validation even though the fields are meant to be mutually exclusive. `age` is in milliseconds, so 0 is realistic.

Nothing requires at least one of the two to be present either, despite the docstrings. Use `"age" in self.initial_data` / `"timestamp" in self.initial_data`, and add a `validate()` that requires exactly one.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same bug: using `.get('timestamp')` (and `.get('age')`) relies on truthiness, which fails when the value is `0` (falsy), allowing both fields to pass the mutual-exclusion check. Both recommend using `'timestamp' in self.initial_data` instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Error timestamps (seconds) are compared with rrweb event timestamps (milliseconds)

`fetch_error_details` takes `timestamp` from the nodestore event payload, which is float seconds since epoch (~1.7e9). `gen_request_data` compares it against the top-level `timestamp` of replay recording events (lines 153-155). The JS SDK writes those in milliseconds (`breadcrumb.timestamp * 1000`, ~1.7e12).

With real data every error looks earlier than every breadcrumb. All errors are emitted at the start of the log instead of being interleaved chronologically, which is the main point of this change. The emitted messages also mix units (`at 1.7e9` for errors, `at 1.7e12` for breadcrumbs), which misleads the LLM.

The tests hide this because they use seconds for both. Convert the error timestamp to milliseconds (`* 1000`) before sorting and comparing, and use ms in the tests.

HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES are only hidden while a search query is entered

The memo returns `sorted` unfiltered when `searchQuery` is empty. The `!HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES.includes(attribute.name)` check only runs in the search branch.

In the default view (no search) `is_segment`, `project_id` and `received` are still shown. They disappear only once the user types something, which is inconsistent and almost certainly not intended. Filter out hidden attributes before the early return.

One invalid report rejects the whole batch, so valid reports are dropped and retried

The endpoint returns 422 as soon as any report in the array fails validation, for example an unlisted or new report type in the strict `ChoiceField`. Per the Reporting API, any non-2xx response marks delivery as failed, and the browser retries the entire batch.

As a result, the valid reports in that batch are never counted, and the same payload is re-sent repeatedly. Consider counting the valid reports and logging or skipping the invalid ones instead of failing the request.

No remaining test exercises the application/reports+json content type

The removed `test_logs_request_data_if_option_enabled` and the old multiple-reports test were the only tests that posted with `content_type="application/reports+json"`. Every test now uses the default JSON format.

The custom `BrowserReportsJSONParser` is the content type real browsers send, and it is no longer covered. A regression in parser registration would go unnoticed. Keep at least one success-path test using that media type.

Data migrations turned into no-ops pointing to a migration not included in this PR

Both 0917 and 0920 now just `return` and point readers to `0921_convert_org_saved_searches_to_views_rerevised.py`. That migration is not added in this PR, and the migrations lockfile is unchanged.

If 0921 does not already exist, organization-visible saved searches are never converted to GroupSearchViews. This affects every environment that has not run these migrations yet, including self-hosted. The comment would also be a dangling reference. Either include the replacement migration or confirm it exists.

Query key omits organization, allowing cached attributes to leak across orgs

The new react-query key is `['use-trace-item-attribute-keys', queryOptions]`. `queryOptions` contains item type, attribute type, project ids and datetime, but not the organization slug, while the queryFn fetches `/organizations/${organization.slug}/...`.

When switching organizations with the same page filters (e.g. `projects: []` for "My Projects" and the same period), the cached attribute keys from the previous org are served until the refetch completes.

This refactor also dropped the previous `retry: false` / `refetchOnWindowFocus: false`, so failures now retry with backoff by default. Include `organization.slug` in the key and restore the intended query options.

Container lost align-items and gap during Flex migration

The removed `Container` was `styled(FlexBox)`, so it had `align-items: center` and `gap: space(1)` in addition to `justify-content: space-between`. The replacement `<Flex ref={setRef} justify="space-between">` sets only the justify.

The tabs and `TraceContextVitals` are no longer vertically centered and have no gap between them, which is a visual regression from what was meant to be a no-op refactor. Add `align="center" gap={space(1)}`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The BrowserReportingCollectorEndpoint returns HttpResponse objects but the endpoint inherits from Endpoint which expects rest_framework.response.Response objects.
In BaseDetectorTypeValidator.update(), the validator incorrectly updates instance.type using validated_data.get('detector_type') instead of validated_data.get('type').

Analytics events are recorded before the feature flag check, resulting in analytics being logged for all requests, including those that return 404 due to the feature being disabled. This can lead to misleading analytics data.

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

true_positives.golden_comment: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.

Inside `group.Go`, each worker assigns to the enclosing function's `err` (`_, _, err = s.build(...)`) and returns it, and also increments `totalBatchesIndexed++` without synchronization.

Before this PR, `bleveBackend.BuildIndex` held `cacheMu` for its entire duration, which effectively serialized most of the work. This PR removes that lock so builds really run in parallel with up to `initWorkers` goroutines, which widens the race window considerably.

This PR removes the `Init` call from all handlers (Create, Update, Delete, Read, List, Watch, Search, History, Origin, IsHealthy, PutBlob, GetBlob), and nothing else reads `initErr`. false_positives.candidate:
Shared queue pool is shut down on first rebalance, then reused: every later message is dropped and committed

`self.queue_pool` is created once in the factory `__init__`, and every `create_with_partitions` call hands that same pool to a new `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy`. On partition revocation, arroyo calls `strategy.close()`/`join()`, which run `queue_pool.shutdown()`. That stops all worker threads and calls `Queue.shutdown()` on every queue.

After the next assignment, the new strategy's `submit` reaches `work_queue.put(...)`, which raises `queue.ShutDown`. The generic `except Exception` in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` catches it, logs it, and marks the offset as added and completed. The commit loop then commits it.

Result: after the first rebalance (any deploy or scale event), the consumer silently discards every uptime result while advancing committed offsets, until the process restarts. The pool (and its offset tracker) needs to be created per assignment, or must not be shut down by the strategy.

Arroyo commit callback invoked from a background thread

`_commit_loop` runs on its own thread and calls `commit_function`, which calls arroyo's `commit`. That is the StreamProcessor's `__commit`, which calls `consumer.stage_offsets()`, `commit_offsets()` and the DLQ policy flush.

Arroyo's StreamProcessor and KafkaConsumer are not thread-safe. Their staged-offset dicts, consumer state machine (ASSIGNING/REVOKING) and commit-policy state are mutated by `poll()` and the rebalance callbacks on the main thread. Calling into them concurrently can corrupt or lose staged offsets, or raise `InvalidState`/`ConsumerError` mid-rebalance.

The `close()` path makes this worse: when the shutdown event is set, the loop still runs one more iteration and commits while the main thread is inside the revoke callback. Offsets should be handed back to the main thread, e.g. committed from `poll()`/`join()`.

Offset tracker never forgets revoked partitions, so commits can fail permanently for all partitions

`OffsetTracker` lives on the shared `FixedQueuePool` and is never cleared or filtered when partitions are revoked. `get_committable_offsets` iterates every partition ever seen, so after a rebalance the committable map can include a partition this consumer no longer owns. This happens whenever completions land after the last commit, and workers keep running after close.

Arroyo's `KafkaConsumer.stage_offsets` raises "cannot stage offsets for unassigned partitions" if any key is unassigned. The commit loop catches that and skips `mark_committed`, so the same stale entry is returned and fails again every second. Commits for all currently assigned partitions are blocked as well.

Separately, outstanding offsets left behind for a revoked partition would block that partition's commits forever if it is later reassigned. Tracker state must be scoped to the current assignment.

Unbounded queues with no backpressure; docstring claims otherwise

Each work queue is `queue.Queue()` with no maxsize, and `submit` never raises `MessageRejected`. The strategy docstring promises "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but nothing applies it.

When any worker is slow or stuck (the exact scenario this PR targets), the main thread keeps polling Kafka at full speed. Messages pile up in memory, each WorkItem holding the full arroyo `Message`. The `OffsetTracker` sets also grow without bound, because commits cannot pass the stuck offset.

At uptime-results volume this can OOM the consumer, and every buffered item is reprocessed after a restart. Bound the queues or the number of outstanding offsets, and raise `MessageRejected` when the limit is exceeded. The docstring claims "No item is lost" and "Only commits offsets after successful processing" are also inaccurate: failures and decode errors are committed.

Commit logic requires contiguous Kafka offsets and stalls forever on a gap

`get_committable_offsets` walks `range(start, max_offset + 1)` and stops at the first offset not in `all_offsets`. After the first commit, `start` is `last_committed + 1`.

Kafka offsets are not guaranteed contiguous: transactional producers write control records, compaction removes offsets, and retention can skip ahead. If an offset is never delivered to `submit`, `highest_committable` never advances again for that partition. Commits stop permanently while the in-memory tracker keeps growing.

Arroyo delivers messages in order per partition, so the tracker should track offsets in arrival order. It can then commit up to (but excluding) the earliest still-outstanding received offset, instead of assuming every integer offset will appear. The new tests (`test_offset_gaps_block_commits`) codify the problematic behavior.

Shutdown blocks up to 5s per worker sequentially and ignores arroyo's join timeout

`FixedQueuePool.shutdown` joins each worker with `timeout=5.0` in sequence. With the default 20 queues, close/join during a rebalance can block for up to 100 seconds, which risks exceeding rebalance/poll timeouts and being kicked from the group. `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join(timeout)` ignores the timeout arroyo passes.

Workers still busy after their join times out keep processing items for partitions that have been revoked. Another consumer may already be processing the same partition, so the same subscription can be handled concurrently and out of order.

In addition, the commit thread is stopped before the workers finish, so results completed during shutdown are never committed and get reprocessed.

Two Sentry transactions started per message

Every work item is wrapped in `sentry_sdk.start_transaction(op="queue_worker.process")`, and `ResultProcessor.__call__` immediately starts another transaction. Each Kafka message therefore produces two transactions, compared with one per batch in batched-parallel mode.

At uptime-results throughput this multiplies tracing volume and overhead. It also adds a per-message `metrics.gauge` call in the `finally` block. A span, or reusing the processor's transaction, would be more appropriate.

Racy/probabilistic assertions make tests flaky

`test_stats_reporting` asserts `stats["total_items"] > 0` right after submitting 10 trivially-fast items. The three worker threads may have already drained the queues, so the assertion can fail nondeterministically.

Similarly, `test_different_groups_distributed` (line 106) assumes 20 keys hashed with the per-process randomized `hash()` always cover all 3 queues. That fails with roughly 0.1% probability depending on PYTHONHASHSEED.

--max-workers help text implies it applies to all parallel modes

The help text now reads "The maximum amount of parallelism to use when in a parallel mode." However, `--mode parallel` ignores `max_workers` and uses `--processes`.

`max_workers` means thread count in batched-parallel mode and number of queues/threads in thread-queue-parallel mode. The text should name the modes it actually affects.
