`AdminPermissionsSchema.getResourceTypeResource(...)` can return null. This happens when the schema is not supported for the current context, or when the "Groups" resource was never created. The result is passed straight into `policyStore.findByResource(server, resource)` and later `resource.getScopes()` with no null check.

`AdminPermissionsSchema.init` returns early if the admin-permissions client already exists. Realms that enabled admin permissions before this change therefore have no "Groups" resource and none of the new `manage-members`/`view-members`/`manage-membership` scopes.

For such realms, any admin without the `view-users`/`manage-users` roles who lists or reads groups goes through `canView(group)` and hits this path, which fails with a 500. Creating group permissions there also fails with "No scopes found".

Add a null guard here, and either add a migration or create the missing schema resources and scopes for existing admin-permissions clients.

Any per-group permission hides all-groups grants for other scopes on that group

`hasPermission` falls back to the all-groups resource only when no per-group resource exists. Once any permission references a group (for example VIEW_MEMBERS on `topGroup`), that group's resource exists and only it is evaluated.

Per-group resources are created without a type, so the "Groups"-typed all-groups permissions are not included in that evaluation. As a result, an admin with "manage all groups" who is also given "view-members on topGroup" can no longer manage, view, or map roles on `topGroup`.

This also makes `canView()`/`canManage()` (all-groups) and `canView(group)`/`canManage(group)` disagree for the same group. The evaluation should combine the per-group result with the all-groups resource for scopes the per-group permissions do not decide.

requireManageMembers Javadoc references the wrong method

The Javadoc for `requireManageMembers(GroupModel)` says it throws ForbiddenException if `canManageMembership(GroupModel)` returns false. The implementations actually check `canManageMembers(GroupModel)`, which is a different scope (MANAGE_MEMBERS vs MANAGE_MEMBERSHIP). It looks copy-pasted from `requireManageMembership` and will mislead callers.

Separately, `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission` documents its return as a "Stream" while it returns a Set.

Public evaluator interface methods renamed/removed without deprecation

`GroupPermissionEvaluator.getGroupsWithViewPermission()` is renamed to `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()`, and `getGroupsWithViewPermission(GroupModel)` is removed. `ModelToRepresentation.searchGroupModelsByAttributes` is also removed.

`GroupPermissionEvaluator` is reachable from `AdminPermissionEvaluator`, which custom admin REST extensions (`AdminRealmResourceProvider`) receive. Those extensions will fail to compile or link after upgrade.

Consider keeping the old method as a deprecated default that delegates to the new one.

Groups resource type not handled in getResourceName

The new GROUPS resource type is added, but `getResourceName` still only maps USERS resources to human-readable names ("All users" or the username).

Per-group resources are created by `getOrCreateResource` with the group id as name and no display name. The "Groups" type resource also has no display name. For group permissions this method therefore returns `resource.getDisplayName()`, which is null.

Resource names shown for group permissions in the admin API/UI will be null or meaningless instead of "All groups" or the group name/path.

testManageGroupMembership does not verify that the group-level permission is required

The test grants all-users MANAGE_GROUP_MEMBERSHIP and per-group MANAGE_MEMBERSHIP together, then only asserts that the join succeeds.

The initial negative check uses the non-existent group "no-such", so it only exercises the user-level check. Nothing asserts that the join to `topGroup` is forbidden when the group's MANAGE_MEMBERSHIP permission is absent, so a regression in `GroupPermissionsV2.canManageMembership` would go unnoticed.

The suite also has no case for all-groups VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS on user listing or count, which would expose the `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission` bug.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract `order()` breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations

`int order()` is added to the public `CryptoProvider` SPI as an abstract method. Any external or custom implementation no longer compiles.

Binaries compiled against the previous `keycloak-common` are worse: when such a provider is discovered, `Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order)` in `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` throws `AbstractMethodError` during the sort. That aborts crypto initialization entirely, even if a valid built-in provider is also present.

A `default int order() { return 0; }` (or similar) would keep the SPI backward compatible while still letting the built-in providers take precedence.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same backward-compatibility issue: adding an abstract order() method to CryptoProvider breaks existing implementations. The candidate provides additional compile-time and runtime consequences of that change.

false_positives.candidate:
Multiple equal-order crypto providers are now silently resolved by classpath order

`detectProvider` used to throw when more than one `CryptoProvider` was found. It now sorts by `order()` and takes the first. `DefaultCryptoProvider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider` and `FIPS1402Provider` all return 200, so a tie between them is broken only by the stable sort, i.e. by `ServiceLoader`/classpath order. The ignored providers are logged at DEBUG only.

Consequence: a deployment that relies on `CryptoIntegration.init` (not `setProvider`) and has both the FIPS and the default crypto jars on the classpath now silently picks one at random instead of failing. It may run in non-FIPS mode without any visible warning.

All discovered providers are also instantiated before sorting. The constructors of `FIPS1402Provider` and `DefaultCryptoProvider` change JVM-global state: they insert BCFIPS/BCJSSE/KeycloakFipsSecurityProvider at positions 1-3, add BC, and rewrite `ssl.KeyManagerFactory.algorithm`. A provider that loses the tie still leaves those changes behind. Before this PR startup aborted in that case.

Suggested fix: keep the hard failure (or at least WARN) when the two highest-ranked providers have the same `order()`, and only drop lower-ranked ones.

ES384/ES512 tests use a P-256 key, so long-form DER lengths are never tested and only a self-roundtrip is checked

The test builds one key pair with `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()`, which defaults to P-256, and reuses it for ES256, ES384 and ES512. With a P-256 key, r and s are at most 33 bytes and the DER SEQUENCE is under 128 bytes. So the long-form length paths in the new `ASN1Encoder.writeLength` and `ASN1Decoder.readLength` (needed for P-521/ES512, where the sequence is about 136-139 bytes) are never executed. The 48- and 66-byte component sizes are only checked as zero padding of 32-byte values.

The test also compares only the output of the hand-written decoder against itself after a round trip through the hand-written encoder. A symmetric encoding bug would pass. It never checks the re-encoded DER with `Signature.verify`, and never compares against a reference implementation such as BC.

Suggested fix: generate a key on the matching curve (secp256r1/secp384r1/secp521r1) for each algorithm, and assert that `signature.verify(asn1Des)` succeeds.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)

Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

true_positives.golden_comment: The reader thread isn’t waited for; flipping deletedAll to true and asserting immediately can race and miss exceptions added just after the flag change, making this test flaky.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reader thread is never joined, so its exceptions can be missed

The test sets `deletedAll` to true and then asserts on `caughtExceptions` right away, without joining the reader thread. At that moment the reader may still be inside a `groups()` request that overlapped the last deletions. An exception from that request is added to the list after the assertion has already passed, so a regression can go undetected. Nothing guarantees the reader issued any request during the deletion window either, so the test may pass without exercising the race at all. Keep a reference to the thread, `join()` it after setting the flag, and ideally check that at least one read overlapped the deletions.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race: the test sets deletedAll and immediately asserts without waiting for the reader thread, allowing exceptions recorded afterward to be missed. The candidate's additional coverage concern does not change this match.

false_positives.candidate:
Same NPE remains in the paginated getSubGroupsStream overloads

The fix null-guards only `getSubGroupsCount()`. The three paginated `getSubGroupsStream(...)` overloads (lines 256, 262, 268) still call `modelSupplier.get().getSubGroupsStream(...)` directly. `modelSupplier.get()` returns null when the group has been deleted in the database but the cached adapter is still in use. That is exactly the concurrent-deletion race this PR targets. Listing or paginating subgroups of a group deleted by another request will still throw a NullPointerException and return HTTP 500. These call sites should get the same null handling, e.g. return `Stream.empty()` when the model is null.

Background thread loops forever if a deletion throws

`deletedAll.set(true)` runs only after every `remove()` call succeeds. If any deletion throws (e.g. a 500 or a 404), the flag is never set. The non-daemon reader thread then keeps calling the admin API in a tight loop indefinitely. It leaks into later tests and can keep the JVM from exiting. Put the deletion loop in try/finally so the flag is always set, and make the thread a daemon or join it.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Returning null from getSubGroupsCount() violates the GroupModel contract (Javadoc says it never returns null) and may lead to NPEs in callers that expect a non-null count.

true_positives.golden_comment: In UsernameForm.authenticate(), isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() is called without passing the required UserModel parameter.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Call to non-existent no-arg isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() breaks compilation

`UsernameForm.authenticate` calls `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` with no arguments. The only method added in the superclass `UsernamePasswordForm` is `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)`, and no no-arg overload exists anywhere in the hierarchy. The services module will not compile, so neither the fix nor the new tests can run. The call should pass the current user, e.g. `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same missing UserModel argument in the call to isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() within UsernameForm.authenticate(). The candidate additionally explains the resulting compilation failure.

true_positives.golden_comment: With isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user) requiring user != null, authenticate(...) will not call webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context) on the initial login page where context.getUser() is still null, so conditional passkey UI will not be set up for first-time passkey login. Consider whether this should also be enabled when no user has been selected yet so ID-less passkey authentication on the initial login form continues to work.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isConditionalPasskeysEnabled requires user != null, disabling passkeys on normal login and enabling them for every re-auth

The new helper returns `webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled() && user != null`. Before this PR, the conditional UI was filled only when no user was selected yet (the normal identity-first login). It is used in `authenticate()` (line 115) and in `challenge(context, error, field)` (line 137), and with this condition:
(1) On a fresh login where `context.getUser()` is null, `fillContextForm` is never called. The webauthn challenge and conditional UI are no longer rendered, so passkey login is broken for all first-time and logged-out logins.
(2) During re-authentication it returns true for any identified user, so the passkey UI is shown even to users with no passkey credential.
The intended condition is `user == null || user.credentialManager().isConfiguredFor(webauthnAuth.getCredentialType())`.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying issue: requiring a non-null user prevents authenticate() from calling fillContextForm on the initial login page, breaking conditional, ID-less passkey login. Its additional re-authentication concern does not change this match.

false_positives.candidate:
Re-auth test for user without passkey disables passkeys realm-wide, so the per-user check is never tested

`reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey` sets `setWebAuthnPolicyPasskeysEnabled(Boolean.FALSE)` for the whole realm. The webauthn form is therefore absent simply because the feature is off, not because the user lacks a passkey. Yet the inline comment at line 304 says passkeys are unavailable "as this user does not have passkey".

The important case is never exercised: passkeys enabled in the realm, and a user without a passkey credential re-authenticating with prompt=login. That case is exactly where the `user != null` logic in `UsernamePasswordForm.isConditionalPasskeysEnabled` misbehaves. The test should keep passkeys enabled and assert the webauthn form is absent for test-user@localhost.

true_positives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Inconsistent metric tag key: 'shards' vs 'shard'

`spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` is tagged with `{"shards": shard_tag}`. `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` use `{"shard": shard_tag}` for the same value. Dashboards that group or filter these flusher metrics by one key will silently miss the other metric.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same inconsistent 'shard' versus 'shards' tag keys on the same metrics and explains the same aggregation and filtering impact.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Added time.sleep(0.1) is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched

The test calls `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)` at the start, so the new `time.sleep(0.1)` does nothing. The comment says it gives the flusher threads time to process the drift change, but it doesn't. The test still races: `join()` sets `stopped=True` and the flusher thread may exit before it ever observes the new drift, which makes the test flaky. A real wait (e.g. the original `sleep` saved before patching, or polling until `messages` is non-empty) is needed.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that time.sleep is monkeypatched to return immediately, making time.sleep(0.1) a no-op instead of the intended wait in test_basic.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Hung flusher processes are no longer killed before a replacement is spawned

The old code called `self.process.kill()` unconditionally. The new code only kills when `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` is true. Processes come from `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process`, which builds `SpawnProcess`. `SpawnProcess` subclasses `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess`, not `multiprocessing.Process` (that is `context.Process`), so the check is always False in production.

When a process is flagged as a `hang`, the still-alive old process is left running and a second process is started for the same shards. Both share the same `stopped`, `current_drift`, `healthy_since` and `backpressure_since` Values. Consequences:
- Two processes can call `flush_segments` on the same shards concurrently and produce duplicate segments to buffered-segments.
- The stale process can keep refreshing `healthy_since`, masking the new one's health.
- Up to MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS orphan processes can leak.

The same broken check at line 346 means `terminate()` in `join()` never runs either. Use `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess` (or check for not being a `threading.Thread`) instead.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying bug: spawn-context processes are SpawnProcess instances, not subclasses of multiprocessing.Process on POSIX, so the isinstance check fails and hung flusher processes are not killed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Added time.sleep(0.1) is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched

The test calls `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)` at the start, so the new `time.sleep(0.1)` does nothing. The comment says it gives the flusher threads time to process the drift change, but it doesn't. The test still races: `join()` sets `stopped=True` and the flusher thread may exit before it ever observes the new drift, which makes the test flaky. A real wait (e.g. the original `sleep` saved before patching, or polling until `messages` is non-empty) is needed.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that time.sleep was monkeypatched to a no-op, so the added sleep does not allow the flusher time to process. Both recommend a real wait or alternative synchronization.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() breaks out of the loop on deadline and skips terminating the remaining processes

In `join()`, once the deadline has passed, `if remaining_time <= 0: break` exits the loop entirely. Every process after that point never reaches the `process.terminate()` call. Before this change, terminate was always attempted after the wait.

With several flusher processes, a timed-out join (e.g. during rebalancing) leaves the later processes running unsupervised. They can keep flushing shards that may now belong to another consumer. A stuck process would never exit, because it is only stopped via the `stopped` flag.

The deadline check should only skip the waiting, not the termination.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: breaking out of the join loop when the deadline expires skips termination of remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown.

false_positives.candidate:
Cluster-wide Redis memory info is queried once per flusher buffer on every submit

`get_memory_info()` reports memory for the whole Redis cluster, not for a shard. The new loop calls it once per per-process buffer, so every `submit()` issues N times as many INFO calls to every cluster node.

The used/available ratio comes out the same only because both sums are multiplied by N. The extra calls are pure overhead on the consumer's main thread, which this PR is trying to keep minimal.

`record_stored_segments` is likewise split into N separate pipelines. Query memory info once (e.g. from a single buffer) instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes the get_multi result preserves the input order; dict value order is not guaranteed to match error_ids, so event data can be paired with the wrong ID (missing nodes also shift alignment).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes nodestore get_multi preserves input order

`nodestore.backend.get_multi` returns a dict keyed by node_id. Its order is not guaranteed to match `error_ids`: cached items come first, then fetched ones, and missing entries may be omitted entirely. Zipping `error_ids` with `events.values()` can therefore attach the wrong event id to each payload, or shift every id after a missing one.

Look up each payload by its generated node_id instead, e.g. `events.get(Event.generate_node_id(project_id, event_id))`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same ordering and alignment bug: zipping error_ids with get_multi dictionary values can pair event payloads with incorrect IDs because result order may differ and missing entries can shift alignment.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoded empty data passed to TableWidgetVisualization causes it to always render an empty table instead of displaying actual results when the feature flag is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Feature-flagged TableWidgetVisualization always renders an empty table

When `use-table-widget-visualization` is enabled, the widget renders `TableWidgetVisualization` with `columns={[]}` and hard-coded empty `tableData`. It ignores `result.data`, `result.meta`, the loading state and the field aliases.

Any org with the flag on sees empty table widgets on every dashboard, with no loading indicator. Map `result` into `TabularData` and columns before gating real users onto this flag.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: when the feature flag is enabled, TableWidgetVisualization receives hardcoded empty data rather than actual results, causing it to render an empty table.

true_positives.golden_comment: Validation logic incorrectly uses .get('timestamp'), which treats a timestamp of 0 as absent. It should directly check 'timestamp' in self.initial_data to ensure proper field presence detection, preventing both 'age=0' and 'timestamp' from passing mutual-exclusion validation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Mutual-exclusion check for age/timestamp uses truthiness

`validate_timestamp` checks `self.initial_data.get("age")` and `validate_age` checks `self.initial_data.get("timestamp")`. A legitimate value of 0 is falsy, so a report carrying both `timestamp` and `age: 0` passes validation even though the fields are meant to be mutually exclusive. `age` is in milliseconds, so 0 is realistic.

Nothing requires at least one of the two to be present either, despite the docstrings. Use `"age" in self.initial_data` / `"timestamp" in self.initial_data`, and add a `validate()` that requires exactly one.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same truthiness-based field-presence bug, explicitly noting that .get("timestamp") treats 0 as absent and recommending membership checks. Its additional concern about requiring one field does not negate the match.

false_positives.candidate:
Error timestamps (seconds) are compared with rrweb event timestamps (milliseconds)

`fetch_error_details` takes `timestamp` from the nodestore event payload, which is float seconds since epoch (~1.7e9). `gen_request_data` compares it against the top-level `timestamp` of replay recording events (lines 153-155). The JS SDK writes those in milliseconds (`breadcrumb.timestamp * 1000`, ~1.7e12).

With real data every error looks earlier than every breadcrumb. All errors are emitted at the start of the log instead of being interleaved chronologically, which is the main point of this change. The emitted messages also mix units (`at 1.7e9` for errors, `at 1.7e12` for breadcrumbs), which misleads the LLM.

The tests hide this because they use seconds for both. Convert the error timestamp to milliseconds (`* 1000`) before sorting and comparing, and use ms in the tests.

HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES are only hidden while a search query is entered

The memo returns `sorted` unfiltered when `searchQuery` is empty. The `!HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES.includes(attribute.name)` check only runs in the search branch.

In the default view (no search) `is_segment`, `project_id` and `received` are still shown. They disappear only once the user types something, which is inconsistent and almost certainly not intended. Filter out hidden attributes before the early return.

One invalid report rejects the whole batch, so valid reports are dropped and retried

The endpoint returns 422 as soon as any report in the array fails validation, for example an unlisted or new report type in the strict `ChoiceField`. Per the Reporting API, any non-2xx response marks delivery as failed, and the browser retries the entire batch.

As a result, the valid reports in that batch are never counted, and the same payload is re-sent repeatedly. Consider counting the valid reports and logging or skipping the invalid ones instead of failing the request.

No remaining test exercises the application/reports+json content type

The removed `test_logs_request_data_if_option_enabled` and the old multiple-reports test were the only tests that posted with `content_type="application/reports+json"`. Every test now uses the default JSON format.

The custom `BrowserReportsJSONParser` is the content type real browsers send, and it is no longer covered. A regression in parser registration would go unnoticed. Keep at least one success-path test using that media type.

Data migrations turned into no-ops pointing to a migration not included in this PR

Both 0917 and 0920 now just `return` and point readers to `0921_convert_org_saved_searches_to_views_rerevised.py`. That migration is not added in this PR, and the migrations lockfile is unchanged.

If 0921 does not already exist, organization-visible saved searches are never converted to GroupSearchViews. This affects every environment that has not run these migrations yet, including self-hosted. The comment would also be a dangling reference. Either include the replacement migration or confirm it exists.

Query key omits organization, allowing cached attributes to leak across orgs

The new react-query key is `['use-trace-item-attribute-keys', queryOptions]`. `queryOptions` contains item type, attribute type, project ids and datetime, but not the organization slug, while the queryFn fetches `/organizations/${organization.slug}/...`.

When switching organizations with the same page filters (e.g. `projects: []` for "My Projects" and the same period), the cached attribute keys from the previous org are served until the refetch completes.

This refactor also dropped the previous `retry: false` / `refetchOnWindowFocus: false`, so failures now retry with backoff by default. Include `organization.slug` in the key and restore the intended query options.

Container lost align-items and gap during Flex migration

The removed `Container` was `styled(FlexBox)`, so it had `align-items: center` and `gap: space(1)` in addition to `justify-content: space-between`. The replacement `<Flex ref={setRef} justify="space-between">` sets only the justify.

The tabs and `TraceContextVitals` are no longer vertically centered and have no gap between them, which is a visual regression from what was meant to be a no-op refactor. Add `align="center" gap={space(1)}`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The BrowserReportingCollectorEndpoint returns HttpResponse objects but the endpoint inherits from Endpoint which expects rest_framework.response.Response objects.
In BaseDetectorTypeValidator.update(), the validator incorrectly updates instance.type using validated_data.get('detector_type') instead of validated_data.get('type').

Analytics events are recorded before the feature flag check, resulting in analytics being logged for all requests, including those that return 404 due to the feature being disabled. This can lead to misleading analytics data.

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative-offset branch slices a QuerySet with a negative index, causing an unhandled error

With `enable_advanced_features=True` and a client-supplied cursor such as `0:-10:0`, the code runs `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative `start_offset`.

Django QuerySets do not support negative indexing; they raise `ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported.")`. The comment claiming "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is false.

`Endpoint.paginate` only converts `BadPaginationError` into a 400. So any client can trigger a 500 by crafting the cursor.

The stated intent, "access to data beyond normal pagination bounds", is also not a legitimate feature. Negative offsets should be rejected with `BadPaginationError`, as `OffsetPaginator` and `ChainPaginator` already do.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same underlying bug: OptimizedCursorPaginator uses negative slice offsets on Django QuerySets, which are unsupported and raise an exception. The differing exception type does not change the issue being identified.

true_positives.golden_comment: When requests are authenticated with API keys or org auth tokens (which have user_id=None), organization_context.member is None. Line 71 attempts to access organization_context.member.has_global_access without checking if member is None, causing an AttributeError crash when optimized_pagination=true is used, even though the request passed all permission checks with valid org:write scope.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unconditional `organization_context.member.has_global_access` crashes when there is no member

`enable_advanced` is computed on every request, even when `optimized_pagination` is not requested. `RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` is optional. It is `None` for callers that pass `OrganizationAuditPermission` without an org membership, for example:
- staff users who are not superusers
- legacy API keys / token-authenticated requests where `request.user` is anonymous

For those callers, `None.has_global_access` raises `AttributeError`, so the previously working default `DateTimePaginator` path now returns a 500.

Fix: guard on `member is not None`, and only evaluate this when `use_optimized` is true.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same unguarded access to organization_context.member.has_global_access when member is None, causing an AttributeError for valid API-key or token-authenticated requests. The candidate additionally claims the default pagination path is affected, but this does not change the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator cannot handle the datetime sort key, so the optimized path always fails

The audit log endpoint uses `OptimizedCursorPaginator` with `order_by="-datetime"`. Its `get_item_key` calls `math.floor`/`math.ceil` directly on `item.datetime`. That raises `TypeError: must be real number, not datetime`.

false_positives.candidate:
Shared queue pool is shut down on first rebalance, then reused: every later message is dropped and committed

`self.queue_pool` is created once in the factory `__init__`, and every `create_with_partitions` call hands that same pool to a new `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy`. On partition revocation, arroyo calls `strategy.close()`/`join()`, which run `queue_pool.shutdown()`. That stops all worker threads and calls `Queue.shutdown()` on every queue.

After the next assignment, the new strategy's `submit` reaches `work_queue.put(...)`, which raises `queue.ShutDown`. The generic `except Exception` in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` catches it, logs it, and marks the offset as added and completed. The commit loop then commits it.

Result: after the first rebalance (any deploy or scale event), the consumer silently discards every uptime result while advancing committed offsets, until the process restarts. The pool (and its offset tracker) needs to be created per assignment, or must not be shut down by the strategy.

Arroyo commit callback invoked from a background thread

`_commit_loop` runs on its own thread and calls `commit_function`, which calls arroyo's `commit`. That is the StreamProcessor's `__commit`, which calls `consumer.stage_offsets()`, `commit_offsets()` and the DLQ policy flush.

Arroyo's StreamProcessor and KafkaConsumer are not thread-safe. Their staged-offset dicts, consumer state machine (ASSIGNING/REVOKING) and commit-policy state are mutated by `poll()` and the rebalance callbacks on the main thread. Calling into them concurrently can corrupt or lose staged offsets, or raise `InvalidState`/`ConsumerError` mid-rebalance.

The `close()` path makes this worse: when the shutdown event is set, the loop still runs one more iteration and commits while the main thread is inside the revoke callback. Offsets should be handed back to the main thread, e.g. committed from `poll()`/`join()`.

Offset tracker never forgets revoked partitions, so commits can fail permanently for all partitions

`OffsetTracker` lives on the shared `FixedQueuePool` and is never cleared or filtered when partitions are revoked. `get_committable_offsets` iterates every partition ever seen, so after a rebalance the committable map can include a partition this consumer no longer owns. This happens whenever completions land after the last commit, and workers keep running after close.

Arroyo's `KafkaConsumer.stage_offsets` raises "cannot stage offsets for unassigned partitions" if any key is unassigned. The commit loop catches that and skips `mark_committed`, so the same stale entry is returned and fails again every second. Commits for all currently assigned partitions are blocked as well.

Separately, outstanding offsets left behind for a revoked partition would block that partition's commits forever if it is later reassigned. Tracker state must be scoped to the current assignment.

Unbounded queues with no backpressure; docstring claims otherwise

Each work queue is `queue.Queue()` with no maxsize, and `submit` never raises `MessageRejected`. The strategy docstring promises "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but nothing applies it.

When any worker is slow or stuck (the exact scenario this PR targets), the main thread keeps polling Kafka at full speed. Messages pile up in memory, each WorkItem holding the full arroyo `Message`. The `OffsetTracker` sets also grow without bound, because commits cannot pass the stuck offset.

At uptime-results volume this can OOM the consumer, and every buffered item is reprocessed after a restart. Bound the queues or the number of outstanding offsets, and raise `MessageRejected` when the limit is exceeded. The docstring claims "No item is lost" and "Only commits offsets after successful processing" are also inaccurate: failures and decode errors are committed.

Commit logic requires contiguous Kafka offsets and stalls forever on a gap

`get_committable_offsets` walks `range(start, max_offset + 1)` and stops at the first offset not in `all_offsets`. After the first commit, `start` is `last_committed + 1`.

Kafka offsets are not guaranteed contiguous: transactional producers write control records, compaction removes offsets, and retention can skip ahead. If an offset is never delivered to `submit`, `highest_committable` never advances again for that partition. Commits stop permanently while the in-memory tracker keeps growing.

Arroyo delivers messages in order per partition, so the tracker should track offsets in arrival order. It can then commit up to (but excluding) the earliest still-outstanding received offset, instead of assuming every integer offset will appear. The new tests (`test_offset_gaps_block_commits`) codify the problematic behavior.

Shutdown blocks up to 5s per worker sequentially and ignores arroyo's join timeout

`FixedQueuePool.shutdown` joins each worker with `timeout=5.0` in sequence. With the default 20 queues, close/join during a rebalance can block for up to 100 seconds, which risks exceeding rebalance/poll timeouts and being kicked from the group. `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join(timeout)` ignores the timeout arroyo passes.

Workers still busy after their join times out keep processing items for partitions that have been revoked. Another consumer may already be processing the same partition, so the same subscription can be handled concurrently and out of order.

In addition, the commit thread is stopped before the workers finish, so results completed during shutdown are never committed and get reprocessed.

Two Sentry transactions started per message

Every work item is wrapped in `sentry_sdk.start_transaction(op="queue_worker.process")`, and `ResultProcessor.__call__` immediately starts another transaction. Each Kafka message therefore produces two transactions, compared with one per batch in batched-parallel mode.

At uptime-results throughput this multiplies tracing volume and overhead. It also adds a per-message `metrics.gauge` call in the `finally` block. A span, or reusing the processor's transaction, would be more appropriate.

`test_stats_reporting` asserts `stats["total_items"] > 0` right after submitting 10 trivially-fast items. The three worker threads may have already drained the queues, so the assertion can fail nondeterministically.

Similarly, `test_different_groups_distributed` (line 106) assumes 20 keys hashed with the per-process randomized `hash()` always cover all 3 queues. That fails with roughly 0.1% probability depending on PYTHONHASHSEED.

The help text now reads "The maximum amount of parallelism to use when in a parallel mode." However, `--mode parallel` ignores `max_workers` and uses `--processes`.

`max_workers` means thread count in batched-parallel mode and number of queues/threads in thread-queue-parallel mode. The text should name the modes it actually affects.

Segment keys written by the previous version are plain Redis sets with TTL up to `redis_ttl` (3600s). After deploy, `ZADD` here, `ZCARD`/`ZUNIONSTORE` in add-buffer.lua, and `ZSCAN` in `_load_segment_data` will hit those keys and fail with `WRONGTYPE`. During a rolling deploy, old consumers likewise run `SADD`/`SCARD` against new ZSET keys. Pipelines raise on the first error, so both the process step and the flusher will crash-loop on any batch or flush touching such a key, potentially for up to an hour until the keys expire. This needs a migration or compat strategy, such as new key prefixes, type-checking with fallback, or draining or flushing the buffer before rollout.

The removed Python code at least emitted `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` and logged an error. Now there is no signal that data was discarded. Eviction is by `end_timestamp_precise` only, so it can also remove the segment/root span when children end after it, while the `hrs` flag still marks the segment as having a root. `zunionstore set_key 2 set_key span_key` (and the same call at line 53) defaults to `AGGREGATE SUM`. If the same span payload exists in both sets, for example after Kafka redelivery or reprocessing a batch, its score becomes the sum of the timestamps (about 2x the end timestamp). That breaks the end-timestamp ordering the new `zpopmin` eviction relies on, and makes such spans effectively un-evictable. Use `AGGREGATE MAX` (or MIN) to keep a real timestamp.

The loop bound for following span redirects drops from 10000 to 1000, and the comment explaining the consequence was removed. The consequence is that segment trees deeper than the limit are not joined correctly. This behavior change is unrelated to eviction, is not mentioned in the PR, and now applies to much shallower trees.

The core behavior change, trimming a segment to 1000 spans via ZPOPMIN by `end_timestamp_precise` including after merges via ZUNIONSTORE, has no test. The existing tests only add `end_timestamp_precise=1700000000.0` to fixtures, with every span sharing the same score, so the eviction order is never exercised. Similarly, the new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` and the audit-log `optimized_pagination` path have no tests, which is how the datetime TypeError and negative-slicing crash went unnoticed.

- Wire up invalidation and use the full sorted id list or a stable digest in the key.

When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache is not re-checked after taking the write lock, so waiting callers reload and overwrite it

In non-dev mode, `GetWebAssets` reads the cache under `RLock`, releases it, and then takes the exclusive `Lock`. It never checks `entryPointAssetsCache` again after acquiring that lock.

At startup, every request that saw a nil cache queues on `Lock()`. Each one then re-opens and re-parses `assets-manifest.json` in turn, although the first holder already filled the cache.

Worse, a later waiter whose read fails transiently runs `entryPointAssetsCache = result` with `result == nil`. That wipes out the good value the earlier goroutine stored and returns an error to that caller. Subsequent requests then have to reload again.

Fix: add the standard double-check after `Lock()`, e.g. `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }`. Optionally, only assign to the cache when `err == nil`.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies that a failed fetch leaves result nil and that assigning it to entryPointAssetsCache overwrites a previously valid cache value, matching the golden issue despite emphasizing the missing double-check.

Without it, a future refactor (for example, removing the TODO'd global state, or adding another unguarded access) could reintroduce the race unnoticed.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup interval changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute (unrelated, likely debug leftover)

The ticker for the whole CleanUpService was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute. The PR description does not mention or justify this.

The interval is coupled to `clean()`'s 9-minute timeout, which was sized to fit inside the 10-minute tick. With a 1-minute tick, a long-running cleanup is followed immediately by the buffered tick, so cleanup can run almost continuously.

The change also affects every cleanup job, not just annotations: temp files, snapshots, dashboard versions, images, invites, short URLs and query history. They now run 10x more often on every Grafana instance (there is no server lock here), which significantly increases database load in HA setups. This should be reverted.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the cleanup ticker changing from 10 minutes to 1 minute and the resulting risk of increased database load from more frequent cleanup execution. The candidate adds details but addresses the same underlying performance concern.

false_positives.candidate:
Bound-parameter IN list can exceed MySQL/Postgres placeholder limits for large batch sizes

The old implementation used a subquery with no bind parameters. The new `deleteByIDs` binds one `?` per ID on every non-SQLite database. MySQL and Postgres both cap prepared statement placeholders at 65535.

Any user who sets `annotation_cleanup_job_batch_size` above 65535 will now get a 'too many placeholders' error on every cleanup run, and annotations will stop being cleaned. Before this change, such a setting worked.

Only SQLite has the inline-values fallback. The batch should be chunked per dialect limit, or the IDs inlined as integers for all dialects (they are int64, so inlining is safe).

Quadratic string building for inline ID list

On the SQLite large-batch path, the IN list is built with `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` in a loop. Each iteration copies the whole accumulated string, so building N IDs is O(N²).

With the batch size used in the new test (32767 IDs, roughly 200KB of text), this copies several gigabytes and creates heavy GC pressure on every batch. A `strings.Builder` or `strings.Join` over `strconv.FormatInt` results makes this linear.

Per-subtest cleanup registered after data creation, so failures leak rows into later subtests

`t.Cleanup` that deletes annotation and annotation_tag rows is registered only after `createTestAnnotations` and the two count assertions. All of these use `require`, which calls `FailNow`.

If insertion or an initial count assertion fails, or if a previous subtest left rows behind, the cleanup is never registered. The rows then remain in the shared DB. Every subsequent subtest then fails its initial count assertion and does not register cleanup either, which cascades failures and hides the original cause. Registering `t.Cleanup` before inserting data avoids this.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes inherit the request context and are canceled when the request ends

Each background goroutine (Create, Update, Delete, DeleteCollection) builds its timeout with `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`, where `ctx` is the incoming request context.

The k8s handlers wrap that context in `context.WithTimeout` and `defer cancel()` it. net/http also cancels the request context as soon as ServeHTTP returns. So once the dual writer returns the storage result, the parent context is canceled almost immediately. The legacy write then races against that cancellation and will often fail with `context canceled`, which leaves legacy storage permanently out of sync.

The 10s timeout adds nothing, because the parent is canceled first. Use `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` as the parent: it keeps request values such as the user identity but drops the cancellation.

Storage create failure is recorded as a legacy metric

When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` instead of `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`.

As a result, storage create errors are reported as legacy-store errors and never show up in the storage error metric. That makes the dual-writer dashboards and alerts misleading.

Storage update failure is recorded as a legacy metric

When `d.Storage.Update` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` with the storage start time. The failure should go to `recordStorageDuration`.

Storage update errors are therefore misattributed to legacy storage and missing from the storage metrics.

Legacy DeleteCollection result recorded via recordStorageDuration

Inside the async goroutine that calls `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection`, the outcome is recorded with `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ..., startLegacy)` instead of `recordLegacyDuration`.

Legacy delete-collection latency and errors are counted as storage metrics. This pollutes the storage series and hides legacy failures.

Legacy update re-applies the raw objInfo instead of the object written to storage

The previous implementation wrapped `objInfo` in `updateWrapper` so legacy received exactly the object persisted in unified storage. The new code passes the original `objInfo` to `d.Legacy.Update` in a background goroutine.

The legacy store then calls `objInfo.UpdatedObject` against its own copy of the old object. For PATCH and server-side apply, the patch is applied to legacy's possibly different state, so the two stores can diverge. The patcher's transformers (patch application, mutating admission) also run a second time, asynchronously, after the request has completed. Keep using `updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: res}` for the legacy write.

Unordered fire-and-forget goroutines can apply legacy writes out of order

Every write spawns an independent goroutine for the legacy write, with no ordering or serialization.

Take a create or update followed quickly by a delete of the same object. The legacy Delete goroutine can run before the earlier Create/Update goroutine finishes. Legacy then ends up with a resurrected or stale object even though unified storage is correct. Because mode 3 never reads from legacy, the divergence goes unnoticed until a rollback to a lower mode. There is also no bound on the number of in-flight goroutines, and `Destroy` does not wait for them.

Legacy write errors are silently dropped (no logging)

In all four async goroutines the legacy error only sets a boolean on a metric; it is never logged. The previous implementation logged legacy failures together with the object.

If legacy writes fail (for example from the context cancellation issue, validation, or conflicts), operators get no error message, object name, or cause to diagnose the divergence. Log `errObjectSt` / `err` with the request logger.

Tests share one mock for both stores and never verify the async legacy write

Both `legacyStoreMock` and `storageMock` wrap the same `mock.Mock`, so the tests cannot tell which store was called.

For example, the "error when creating object in the unified store fails" case only configures `setupLegacyFn`. It passes only because the storage Create call matches the expectation registered for legacy.

No test checks that:
- the legacy write is actually issued after a successful storage write,
- it is skipped when storage fails,
- Get and List never touch legacy.

The background goroutines also outlive the test. The core mode 3 behavior is effectively untested, which is how the canceled-context and metric bugs got through.

Duplicate and unrelated go.work.sum entries

The diff re-adds `github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery v0.0.0-20240701135906-559738ce6ae1/go.mod`, which is already present on the line above. It also adds a number of unrelated dependency checksums (azure sdk, alertmanager, older otel exporters). This is accidental churn from a local `go work sync` and should be dropped from a dual-writer change.

This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

The list view now renders `RuleActionsButtons` with only `promRule` and no ruler rule. `AlertRuleMenu` still shows "Silence notifications", because `canSilence` is true via `useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities`. Clicking it calls `setShowSilenceDrawer(true)`.

The new GrafanaGroupLoader test checks that the silence item exists but never clicks it, so the bug is not caught. The drawer needs to work from the prom rule (e.g. by uid/labels), or the menu item should be hidden when no ruler rule is available.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same issue: list views pass only promRule, so the silence menu is enabled by Grafana Prom abilities but clicking it cannot render the drawer because the required Grafana Ruler rule is absent.

false_positives.candidate:
skipToken still reports Duplicate as supported, enabling Duplicate for data-source rules via Grafana permissions

With `skipToken`, `useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` receives `undefined`. In that case `useIsGrafanaPromRuleEditable` returns `loading: false`, so `MaybeSupported` becomes `AlwaysSupported`. Duplicate then resolves to `toAbility(true, AlertingRuleCreate)`, meaning `[true, true]` for any user with the global Grafana rule create permission.

`AlertRuleMenu` ORs this with the ruler result: `canDuplicate = rulerDuplicate || grafanaDuplicate`. For a data-source-managed rule (which always gets skipToken), Duplicate is therefore shown whenever the user can create Grafana rules. This holds even when the ruler is unavailable (e.g. vanilla Prometheus) or the user lacks external rule write permission. It affects the rule viewer, RulesTable and the v2 list.

When the rule is skipped, the hook should return `[false, false]` for every action.

Delete and Pause actions silently disappear from the list view

Both menu items still require a ruler rule:
- Pause: `canPause && rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule) && ...` (line 123)
- Delete: `canDelete && rulerRule`

The list view (`GrafanaRuleListItem`) no longer passes a ruler rule. So even when the prom-based abilities say the user can pause or delete, these items are never rendered. Previously both actions were available from the list.

`canPause` also still feeds `showDivider`, so a divider can appear without a pause item. The new GrafanaGroupLoader test grants delete permissions yet asserts exactly 4 menu items, which locks this regression in.

Either support pause/delete from the prom rule (identifier + groupIdentifier are available) or document the removal explicitly.

Federated rule groups are no longer treated as immutable

`useAllAlertRuleAbilities` used to compute `isFederated = isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)`, which made Mimir federated groups (those with `source_tenants`) non-editable and non-deletable.

It now delegates to `useAllRulerRuleAbilities`, which hardcodes `const isFederated = false`. All existing consumers of `useAllAlertRuleAbilities`/`useAlertRuleAbility` (rule details, RulesTable, rule viewer) will now offer Update/Delete/Pause for federated rules. Editing those through the UI was previously blocked deliberately.

The federated check should be kept in the CombinedRule path, e.g. by passing the group or a flag.

Prom-based abilities exclude Grafana recording rules from Export/Pause/Restore

The ruler version gates ModifyExport, Pause, Restore and DeletePermanently on `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rule)`, which is true for any Grafana-managed rule including recording rules.

The new prom version uses `isAlertingRule = prometheusRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` for all of these, despite the comment saying "All GrafanaPromRuleDTO rules are Grafana-managed by definition".

In the list view, which now relies only on these prom abilities, Grafana recording rules lose the Export menu item, and Pause/Restore are reported as unsupported. Only Silence should be restricted to alerting rules; the others should use `prometheusRuleType.grafana.rule(rule)`.

Rule view link lost the `returnTo` parameter

The removed implementation built the rule link as `createRelativeUrl(`/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view`, { returnTo })` using `createReturnTo()`. The new component drops `returnTo`.

After opening a rule from the list (including a filtered search), the rule viewer's back navigation can no longer return the user to the same list/filter state. This is a UX regression unrelated to removing ruler requests.

Stale doc comment says the group is loaded from the Ruler endpoint

The JSDoc still reads "Loads an evaluation group from Prometheus and Ruler endpoints", but this PR removed the ruler query. The component now only uses `useGetGrafanaGroupsQuery`.

The `expectedRulesCount` comment also still refers to the Ruler response. Similarly, `prometheusGroupsGenerator.ts` still says "preload ruler rules" and names the variable `cacheAndRulerPreload`, though no ruler prefetch happens anymore.

Queries that interpolate to an empty expr are no longer dropped, which can leave the shard observable hanging

The old code interpolated first and then ran `.filter((query) => query.expr)`. The new code filters on the raw `expr` and only then calls `applyTemplateVariables`. A query such as `expr: '$var'` whose variable resolves to an empty string now passes the filter and comes out with `expr: ''`.

What happens next:
- `groupTargetsByQueryType` puts it in the `otherQueries` group, because `requestSupportsSharding` rejects empty exprs.
- `runNextRequest` calls `runSplitQuery` with that group. `runSplitQuery` filters out empty exprs, so `requests` is `[]`.
- `runSplitGroupedQueries` then throws synchronously at `requests.filter(...)[0].partition` (querySplitting.ts line 96).
- The throw happens inside the `.then()` of `groupTargetsByQueryType`, so it becomes an unhandled promise rejection. The subscriber is never completed or errored, and the panel stays in loading state forever.

This triggers when the request has a shardable query plus a non-shardable query whose variable is empty. Fix: filter `query.expr` after interpolation, here and in `runSplitQuery`, as the previous implementation did.

applyTemplateVariables (including ad-hoc filters) now runs multiple times per query

`runSplitQuery` now calls `datasource.applyTemplateVariables(query, request.scopedVars, request.filters)`. Each sub-request then goes through `datasource.runQuery` → `DataSourceWithBackend.query`, which calls `applyTemplateVariables` again with the same `request.filters`. In the shard path, `runShardSplitQuery` interpolates as well, so each query is processed three times.

Loki's `applyTemplateVariables` is not idempotent: it calls `addAdHocFilters`, which appends ad-hoc filters to the expression. Stream-selector placement de-duplicates via `labelExists`. For queries with a parser (e.g. `{app="x"} | json`), filters go through `addFilterAsLabelFilter`, which has no dedup. The result is queries like `| level=`error` | level=`error` | level=`error`` sent to Loki and shown in the inspector.

Variable values containing `$name` text, and ad-hoc filter values, are also re-interpolated on each pass. The previous shard code deliberately used `interpolateVariablesInQueries` without filters, leaving ad-hoc filter application to the backend-query step.

The updated test asserting `applyTemplateVariables` is called 5 times codifies this redundant processing. Consider interpolating only variables (no `filters`) here, or marking targets as already interpolated so later passes skip ad-hoc injection.

New interpolation test relies on a mock that interpolates `$__auto`, which the real code never does

The test's `replace` mock replaces `$__auto` unconditionally and ignores the scopedVars passed in. The real `LokiDatasource.applyTemplateVariables` explicitly strips `__auto`, `__interval`, `__range`, etc. from scopedVars so they pass through to the backend. In production, `$__auto` therefore stays uninterpolated at this stage.

The test asserts behaviour that cannot happen with the real template service. It also does not check what the change is supposed to fix: that splitting decisions (log vs. metric partitioning, `calculateStep` grouping by `step`) are made on interpolated values.

The same pattern is copied into `shardQuerySplitting.test.ts`. Use a regular dashboard variable and assert on the grouping or partition outcome instead.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Check-then-insert lets concurrent requests exceed the device limit

`CreateOrUpdateDevice` runs `CountDevices` and then a separate upsert, with no transaction or lock around them.

Concurrent first requests from different devices can all read `count < deviceLimit` and all insert. This is especially likely across multiple Grafana instances sharing the DB, or a burst of new visitors. The stored device count can therefore exceed the configured limit.

If the limit is meant as a hard cap, the count and insert need to be atomic, for example a conditional `INSERT ... SELECT` with a count predicate or a serialized transaction.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same check-then-insert race: concurrent requests can pass the device count check and create devices beyond the limit because the check and write lack transaction or locking protection.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device limit bypassed because rejected devices are cached as already tagged

`tagDeviceUI` writes the device key into `localCache` (29-minute TTL) before calling `CreateOrUpdateDevice`. When the store returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, the key stays cached.

The device's next request hits the cache, `tagDeviceUI` returns nil, and `Anonymous.Authenticate` grants access. The limit is enforced only on the first request from a new device; a reload or retry gets in.

The same ordering means a transient DB error suppresses re-tagging for 29 minutes. Fix: on `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, cache a negative marker and return the error on later cache hits. On any other error, delete the key.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same cache-ordering bug: tagDeviceUI caches the device ID before CreateOrUpdateDevice, and ErrDeviceLimitReached leaves that entry intact, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit for the 29-minute TTL.

false_positives.candidate:
ProvideAnonDBStore signature change likely breaks the Wire dependency graph

Before this PR, `ProvideAnonymousDeviceService` took an `anonstore.AnonStore` argument, so the Wire set (pkg/server/wire.go or the enterprise wireexts) must contain `anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore` plus a `wire.Bind` to `AnonStore`. That file is not in this PR.

`ProvideAnonDBStore` now needs an `int64`, which Wire cannot supply. If the provider stays in the set, code generation fails with either a missing int64 provider or an unused-provider error.

If another component still injects `anonstore.AnonStore`, it would get a second store instance that silently ignores the limit. Update or remove the Wire provider and binding in the same change.

Limit keyed on a client-supplied header: trivially bypassed and abusable for lockout

Enforcement relies entirely on the `X-Grafana-Device-Id` header, which the client controls.

1. A request without the header returns nil from `TagDevice` and is authenticated anonymously. Unparseable IPs also return nil. So any non-browser client skips the limit entirely.
2. An unauthenticated attacker can send requests with random device IDs until `device_limit` is reached. Every new legitimate anonymous visitor is then rejected for up to 30 days, until rows age out of the `updated_at` window.

At minimum, document this behaviour. Ideally, rate-limit device creation or treat a missing device ID consistently with the limit.

Device tagging moved onto the synchronous auth path even when no limit is configured

Tagging used to run in a background goroutine with its own timeout and panic recovery. It now runs inline in `Authenticate` using the request context.

Every cache-miss anonymous request now waits for the DB upsert, plus a `COUNT(*)` when a limit is set, before it is authenticated. This applies even with the default `device_limit = 0`, where nothing needs to be enforced.

The panic recovery is also gone, and a client disconnect now cancels the write. Consider staying asynchronous when `AnonymousDeviceLimit == 0`.

Tests don't cover existing devices at the limit or repeated requests from rejected devices

`TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit` only checks that a second new device is rejected.

It does not check that an already-registered device can still update once the limit is reached, which is the `updateDevice` path's main purpose. No test at the service or client level checks that a rejected device stays rejected on later requests, and such a test would have caught the local-cache bypass.

`Anonymous.Authenticate` returning an error on `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is also untested.

anonymousDeviceLimit is inferred as type `undefined` on GrafanaBootConfig

`anonymousDeviceLimit = undefined;` has no type annotation, so TypeScript infers the property type as literal `undefined`, not `number | undefined`.

At runtime the backend sends a number, which is merged into the config. Code that reads `config.anonymousDeviceLimit` and treats it as a number, such as `config.anonymousDeviceLimit > 0`, will not type-check.

Declare it as `anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined = undefined;`.

New device_limit setting not documented in defaults.ini/sample.ini or the docs

`[auth.anonymous] device_limit` is read here, but conf/defaults.ini, conf/sample.ini and the configuration docs are not updated.

Operators have no way to discover the option. Nothing tells them that exceeding it makes new anonymous visitors fail authentication.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

true_positives.golden_comment: Consider normalizing the input locale (e.g., to a symbol) when checking/loading here to avoid double-loading if the same locale is passed as a String vs Symbol (also applies to other locations in the PR).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
FallbackLocaleList does not normalize locale to a symbol

`I18n::Locale::Fallbacks` normally calls `to_sym` on the locale it is given; this replacement does not. When a caller passes `locale: 'en'` (a String), the result is `['en', :fr, :en]`. `uniq` does not remove the duplicate, so the same locale is looked up twice.

In `ensure_loaded!` a string locale would also miss the `@loaded_locales.include?` check, which stores symbols. Use `[locale.to_sym, ...]` (guarding for nil) before `uniq`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify missing locale normalization between Strings and Symbols, causing duplicate locale handling and bypassing the loaded-locale check, potentially loading the same locale twice.

false_positives.candidate:
Translation cache key ignores the site-dependent fallback chain

The LRU cache key is built only from key, `config.locale` and the backend object_id. With the new Fallbacks module, the value returned for a locale also depends on `SiteSetting.default_locale`, which `FallbackLocaleList#[]` reads on every lookup. That setting differs per site in multisite and can be changed by an admin at runtime.

The cache is process-wide, so the first fallback result is stored and reused for everyone. Example: an `:es` user on site A (default `:fr`) hits a key missing in `es`, and the French text is cached. An `:es` user on site B (default `:de`) then gets French instead of German. After an admin changes `default_locale`, stale fallback text is served until `I18n.reload!`.

A 'translation missing' result, or an `en` result produced before the site locale was loaded, is also cached permanently. The cache key should include the fallback chain (or at least `SiteSetting.default_locale`), or fallback results should not be cached.

Fallback locales are only loaded in the controller before_filter

Translations are lazy-loaded per locale. `translate` only calls `load_locale(config.locale)`. The fallback locales (site default and `:en`) are loaded only by `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` in `ApplicationController#set_locale`.

Any code path that translates outside a controller request gets no loaded fallbacks. That includes Sidekiq jobs, mailers run from jobs, rake tasks, and code that sets `I18n.locale` or uses `I18n.with_locale`. When `I18n::Backend::Fallbacks` iterates over those unloaded locales it finds nothing and returns 'translation missing'. Because of the LRU cache, that result is then stuck for the process.

- The controller loop: oversized image is reduced, conversion failure, animated GIF, SVG.

- a missing TopicUser,
- the slug redirect,

`workingHours.find(...)` returns true, meaning the slot is rejected, as soon as any single entry covering that weekday does not contain the slot. It does not check whether at least one entry contains it.

Users routinely have several entries for the same day:
- Split availability, e.g. 9-12 and 13-17.
- Hours that cross UTC midnight, which `getWorkingHours` splits into two entries with shifted `days`. For example, US Pacific 9am-6pm becomes ~16:00-24:00 UTC plus 00:00-01:00 UTC.

A 14:00 slot is outside the 9-12 entry and gets rejected. Each Pacific-time slot is outside one of its two UTC fragments, so every slot is rejected.

The logic should require the slot to be inside at least one applicable range (`some`), not reject it if it is outside any one range.

When a date override matches the slot's day and the slot is not rejected, `if (dateOverrideExist) return true;` returns before the `busy.every(...)` check runs.

On any day with a date override, the user's existing Cal bookings, external calendar events and buffers are therefore ignored. Slots that overlap them are shown as available, for both fixed and round-robin hosts, inviting double bookings or failures at booking time.

Multiple date-override ranges on the same day reject slots inside any range but the first

`dateOverrides.find(...)` returns true, so the slot is marked unavailable, as soon as one override on that day does not contain the slot. Cal.com lets a date override have several time ranges, e.g. 9-10 and 14-15.

A 14:00 slot is checked against the 9-10 override first. `slotStartTime.isAfter(end)` is true, so the slot is rejected even though it lies within the 14-15 range.

Slots on Apr 17 UTC, i.e. the fixed host's whole IST working day, never match the override and fall through to the working-hours check, so they are shown as bookable. That defeats the purpose of this PR for fixed hosts. In the other direction, a slot at Apr 17 20:00Z (Apr 18 01:30 IST) is compared against the Apr 17 override and wrongly rejected.

2. Server timezone dependence. The left side is formatted in the server's local timezone while the right side is UTC, so results change on servers not running in UTC.

- Bookings or busy calendar time on a date-override day.
- Multi-range overrides.
- Working hours with split ranges or ranges crossing UTC midnight.
- "Unavailable" (00:00-00:00) overrides for a non-UTC host.

The existing IST 9:30-18:00 fixture maps to a single UTC range and a single override, so serious regressions in `checkIfIsAvailable` pass unnoticed: whole-day loss of slots, skipped busy times, and wrong day matching.

When `allCodesUsed()` is true, the code still calls `credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(id)`. That only touches Keycloak's local/federated JPA credential store, never the user storage provider.

For a provider-supplied credential this has two failure modes:
- If the id belongs to the provider, the call is a silent no-op. The exhausted credential stays, and `isConfiguredFor` keeps returning true.
- If the provider returns a model without an id, the call receives null. `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues` leaves the id unset, and the test provider's `getCredentials` does exactly this. With a null id, `em.find(..., null)` in the JPA store throws `IllegalArgumentException`, so the login fails with a 500.

For federated credentials the code should take a different path, such as `disableCredentialType(RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE)` or no removal at all.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same root cause: RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues leaves the credential id unset, so a null id is passed to removeStoredCredentialById and downstream removal fails. The candidate adds broader federated-storage context, but it explicitly includes this null-id failure mode.

Old local recovery codes stay valid when new codes are stored in user storage

Before this change, `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.createCredential` always ran, and it deletes the user's existing stored recovery-codes credential before creating the new one. Now, when `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)` returns true (the codes went to user storage), the local provider is skipped, so any previously stored local recovery-codes credential is never deleted.

`UserCredentialManager.isValid` checks the user-storage validator first and then falls through to the local `CredentialInputValidator`s. So a code the user entered that fails in user storage is then checked against the stale local codes and is accepted.

Result: after a user regenerates recovery codes (for example after an upgrade where the provider starts accepting this type, or after a provider config change), the old codes that were supposed to be replaced can still be used to log in. The user-storage branch should also remove any existing local recovery-codes credential.

Test provider accepts any of the codes and never consumes them, so single-use is untested

`isValid` for recovery codes returns true if the input matches any stored code. It never marks the code as used and does not check that it is the code the login form asked for (`getNextRecoveryAuthnCode`).

The new `testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin` therefore only checks that some valid code is accepted once. It would still pass if:
- the wrong code number were entered,
- a code could be reused,
- the next login asked for the same code again.

The core recovery-code contract (single-use, sequential) is not exercised at all for the user-storage path.

Changing the "4.8.3-compatible" provider alters what existing OTP backward-compat tests cover

The class Javadoc says this provider mimics a Keycloak 4.8.3 implementation and should not need changes for newer versions. This PR adds the newer `getCredentials` API and gives OTP credentials a generated id (`newOTP.setId(...)`).

As a result, the existing OTP tests no longer run against an old-style provider. For example, `testOTPSetupAndRemoveThroughAccountMgmtAndLogin` (issue 19575) used to get the placeholder `otp-id` from the account REST endpoint (`CredentialHelper.createUserStorageCredentialRepresentation`). It will now receive the real OTP credential with a UUID from `getFederatedCredentialsStream`.

The legacy placeholder path that these tests were written to protect loses coverage. The recovery-code support would be better placed in a separate, modern test provider.

New feature changes `--features` help output but approved help snapshots are not updated

Adding `ROLLING_UPDATES` adds `rolling-updates[:v1]` to the 'Possible values' list that the `--features` option prints in CLI help. That list is checked by the approval-based help tests (`HelpCommandDistTest.*.approved.txt` for start, start-dev, build, export, import, update-compatibility, etc.). None of those snapshot files are part of this PR, so the help tests are likely to fail once this merges. Regenerate and commit the approved help files together with the new feature.

Operator doc says the Operator will fail without `rolling-updates`, but nothing enforces this

The new CAUTION block says the `rolling-updates` feature must be enabled or 'the Keycloak Operator will fail'. This PR adds no Operator code that checks the feature. The existing `Recreate` strategy behaves the same whether or not the feature is on.

The default `<not set>` strategy also clearly works without the feature: `UpgradeTest` runs the `null` strategy case without enabling it. The statement is therefore inaccurate at this commit. Readers will also be confused about whether the feature is needed when they don't set `update.strategy`.

Hard-coded `--features=rolling-updates` in the command template can clobber the user's real feature set

The `updatecompatibility` macro now appends `--features=rolling-updates` to every documented `update-compatibility` invocation. The same guide tells users to pass exactly the options used by `start`.

Users who already run with `--features=<their list>` will now pass a second `--features` value that replaces their list. The metadata/check then runs with a different feature set than the real deployment, or the duplicate option causes a CLI error. Users need to add `rolling-updates` to their existing list, not override it.

Separately, `features` is a build-time option. With an optimized (`--optimized`) image, passing it at runtime does not take effect. The commands will then exit with code 4 unless the image was rebuilt with the feature, which is why `Dockerfile-custom-image` had to be changed. Neither point is documented.

`testFeatureNotEnabled` only asserts the error text for the `metadata` subcommand. The PR's main contract change is the new exit code `FEATURE_DISABLED = 4` (and the move of `RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE` from 4 to 3), and scripts are told to rely on these exit codes.

No test asserts that a disabled feature yields exit code 4, that `check` is also gated, or that an incompatible result now returns 3. A regression in the exit codes would go unnoticed. Add `assertEquals(CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED, result.exitCode())` for both subcommands, and assert 3 in `testWrongVersions`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.
